Sports.title: 'Biggest moment of my career' - Emotional Menzies reflects on Humphries win
Sports.content:
An emotional Cameron Menzies dubbed his win against Luke Humphries "the biggest moment of my darts career" after his dramatic upset secured his place in the next round of the World Matchplay Darts.

Menzies pulled out an incredible Big Fish checkout to beat world No 2 Humphries 10-7 in his first-ever triumph at Winter Gardens.

The monumental victory was a full-circle moment for the Scot, and represents a remarkable turnaround in fortune just eight months after he required surgery for punching a table during his first-round defeat to Josh Manby at the World Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron Menzies lands the Big Fish finish to stun Luke Humphries at the World Matchplay.

"I don't know how to explain that [victory]. I did believe in my heart that I could maybe cause an upset but I would have to play it out of my skin," Menzies said.

"I wouldn't say I played it out of my skin, but I played really well. I did say before the game started, to beat Luke, I need to take every chance that he gives me.

"It's not like Luke to give a lot of chances away but obviously I'm going to take it. A lot went in. I was happy. I stole a few legs to win but it's made the best moment of my darts career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron Menzies hits a HUGE double-double finish against Luke Humphries!

The Scot revealed in February that he considered giving up darts altogether, but reflected on his greatest ever win after a "terrible" start to 2026, which also included the death of his uncle:

"It's up there because I didn't think I was going to qualify for this.

"The start of the year, I was terrible. I was just really bad. I had a really poor start to the year but I went through a lot.

"I'm in a better place mentally and physically. I'm enjoying darts again."

Mardle: Menzies knows he can handle anything now

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hear from Cameron Menzies and Wayne Mardle after the Scotsman claimed a famous win over Luke Humphries at the World Matchplay.

Sky Sports Darts' Wayne Mardle:

"It's his best ever win, and he mentioned that.

"With Cameron Menzies, everyone mentions his emotions, but it's the way he had to win that game.

"Nothing went according to plan. He was broken back early twice, that's up and down emotions. The high of breaking to being broken back.

Image: Menzies' win against Humphries was his first at Winter Gardens

"Then he went on a run, and got pegged back.

"There was a lot happening in that game, but he held it all together beautifully.

"Humphries had an amazing spell of four legs, but then Menzies found a level again, and that's something we don't see enough.

"What he should take away from tonight was the way he handled this situation. It was like he was there a million times before.

"He knows he can handle anything now."

What's happening at the World Matchplay on Tuesday?

Image: Luke Littler, World Matchplay Darts 2026

The 2026 Betfred World Matchplay continues at the iconic Winter Gardens from July 18-26, as a 32-player field compete for the prestigious Phil Taylor Trophy.

Two-time world champion Luke Littler takes on Nathan Aspinall in a blockbuster clash after opening his defence of the Phil Taylor Trophy with a sensational 10-6 win over Niko Springer on Day One in Blackpool.

Betfred World Matchplay - Tuesday's fixtures [first to 11 legs]

Betfred World Matchplay - Tuesday's fixtures [first to 11 legs] Jonny Clayton vs Gary Anderson Michael van Gerwen vs Dirk van Duijvenbode Luke Littler vs Nathan Aspinall Josh Rock vs Stephen Bunting

Stephen Bunting takes on Josh Rock after winning through a Winter Gardens classic against debutant Niels Zonneveld, surviving three match darts to edge past the Dutchman 13-12.

Three-time World Matchplay winner Michael van Gerwen faces fellow Dutchman Dirk van Duijvenbode, while Gary Anderson - the 2018 champion - goes up against 2023 runner-up Jonny Clayton having recorded the eighth-highest average in World Matchplay history, averaging 109.96 in his 10-2 demolition of Ryan Joyce.

Sports.title: 'We know a lot of what's going on' - Rahm tight-lipped on LIV future
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm has remained tight-lipped about his LIV Golf future for 2027, saying "we know a lot of what's going on" but he is not in a position to share details.

The future of the breakaway golf league beyond the end of this season remains in doubt after the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund confirmed in April it is ending its funding for the series.

As one of the league's highest-profile players, Rahm's future beyond this season has been the subject of speculation amid LIV's bid to seek alternative investment.

LIV is in the UK this week for its event at the JCB Golf and Country Club in Staffordshire, its first tournament since the start of June.

Asked in Tuesday's pre-event press conference whether he had any clarity about LIV's future heading into 2027, Rahm said: "Yes. Well, we're in contact with them.

"We know a lot of what's going on, yeah.

"Not that I can share with you guys right now."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the moment New Zealand's Ryan Fox won The Open with a 12ft birdie putt on the 18th hole at Royal Birkdale

Put to him that he seemed optimistic, the Spaniard said: "I'm always optimistic.

"I play a game for a living. I can't really be too upset about how things are going in life. Even though I'm very frustrated on the course very often, off the course I'm very different to what a lot of people think."

Rahm, who joined the league from the start of 2024, was then asked directly whether he expected to be playing on LIV next year.

"I'm not going to share anything that I can't share with you guys right now," he replied.

Rahm wants clarity over code of conduct warnings

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm received a code of conduct warning at The Open after throwing his club following his tee shot on the par-three 15th at Royal Birkdale

Rahm returns to LIV action after finishing tied 46th at The Open last week after shooting four-over for his final round.

The Spaniard received a code of conduct warning from Friday's second round at Royal Birkdale last week after throwing his club following his tee shot on the par-three 15th.

Asked whether he had sufficient clarity on what actions constitute a warning or a two-shot penalty under the new-for-2026 major code of conduct rules, Rahm said: "I personally have no idea what the line is. No clue."

He added: "I think you can all kind of understand what it may or may not be. I completely forgot about it until it happened. I know they issued multiple warnings over the course of the week.

"Yeah, it would be nice to have some clarity."

Asian Tour announces partnership with PGA and DP World Tours

Image: David Puig of Spain played on the LIV sponsored 'international series', organised by the Asian Tour

The Spaniard was speaking on the same day that the Asian Tour announced a new deal with the DP World Tour and PGA Tour, simultaneously threatening their ties with LIV, with whom they have shared a lucrative partnership with since 2022.

The PGA Tour and DP World Tour have a separate alliance that has yet to be renewed, which includes 10 top European Tour players earning PGA Tour cards, but the alliance with the Asian Tour - along with the PGA Tour's involvement with the Australian Open - is seen as progress on a new deal.

LIV - who will see the announcement as a blow - invested $300m in the Asian Tour to create the "International Series" with purses of up to $2m. They have been won by LIV players such as Peter Uihlein, Carlos Ortiz and David Puig.

"We feel the time is now right to collaborate with the DP World Tour and PGA Tour to enhance the Asian Tour for our members, fans and partners," said Cho Minn Thant, commissioner and CEO of the Asian Tour.

"Bringing the three tours together under one partnership will increase the bandwidth of the professional game in Asia.

"Not only will co-sanctioning events see our members competing regularly on the global stage, but we are excited to welcome players from the other Tours to our pinnacle events."

Sports.title: Charges and challenges - the scale of the task facing Maresca at Man City
Sports.content:
Plenty of the Premier League's top clubs have rolled the managerial dice ahead of next season. Manchester City are one of those starting a new era, turning to Enzo Maresca in the wake of Pep Guardiola's decision to depart.

Maresca is returning for his third stint at the club, having been an academy coach in 2020-21 and then Guardiola's assistant in 2022-23 - the famous Premier League-Champions League-FA Cup treble-winning campaign.

He is familiar with the pursuit of silverware, but is yet to be the one to deliver it at such scale. So, how well positioned is he to lead Man City to glory in 2026-27?

Sky Sports' Ben Ransom and Laura Hunter explore Maresca's chances of success in year one - and whether trophies are the only barometer by which he will be judged in the wake of Guardiola's seismic exit.

Sympathetic start gives Maresca breathing room

Maresca has been given a kind start to his term, meeting Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Coventry City in his first three outings - a generous run to be able to establish some early rhythm. It also gives Man City's World Cup warriors, those in battle until the very last, a chance to ease back in.

Rodri played nearly every minute of Spain's triumphant campaign and is the most susceptible to breaking down with fatigue. Given those first three fixtures will still heavily favour Man City without him, he should benefit from a phased return.

Maresca will, however, be under pressure to deliver given how winnable those fixtures are on paper. He cannot afford to cede ground early, especially as City face Man Utd and Liverpool in two of the next three in September. Clearly both of those rival bouts hold significance beyond the result.

As the Italian acknowledged when joining, he is in a "dream situation", inheriting a well-balanced squad with incredible talent and depth, built by Guardiola. "It provides the consistency I need to do my job effectively," he said.

The demands will therefore be the same as what were placed on Guardiola, without necessarily having the unique job security the Spaniard was afforded. Guardiola always managed on his own terms. Maresca has a strong bond with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, but won't necessarily get the same privilege.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports football journalist Laura Hunter says Enzo Maresca won't be afforded time to excel as Manchester City boss

How much time will players need to adapt?

In terms of style, it's not quite rinse and repeat but there are plenty of similarities between Maresca and Guardiola's preferred way of playing.

Both are rooted in possessing the ball, favouring control, and pressing aggressively. Maresca is arguably more expansive, though, wanting to stretch the pitch with wingers that play high and wide.

Image: Chelsea's stats in their only full season under Enzo Maresca

City's wingers have been coached more recently to play a style where they tuck inside and rotate to create central overloads. Most of the play revolves around Rodri, but it's fluid.

Watching City under Guardiola often meant seeing defenders step into midfield, midfielders become forwards, or even drop into full-back. Maresca's more rigid 4-2-3-1 structure will likely make for more traditional roles.

It also requires a high-functioning No 10 to link play. At Chelsea, that was Cole Palmer. Maresca has got Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki to choose between, should he wish to adopt the same setup here.

How is the squad shaping up?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom explains why Manchester City decided to sign Elliot Anderson for £116m, making him the most expensive British player in history

There has been a concerted effort over the past two or three transfer windows under Hugo Viana to lower the average age of the squad. It's dropped from 29 to just over 25, albeit a leadership void has appeared following the departures of Bernardo Silva and John Stones this summer - and Kevin de Bruyne before them.

Rodri and Ruben Dias are important, while last season saw City lean further into a leadership role for Erling Haaland. Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol are also experienced, stable figures, plus Mateo Kovacic. The spine of the team remains incredibly strong.

Business to date has been costly but smart. Elliot Anderson, signed for mega money from Nottingham Forest, has been bought to add robustness and future-proof midfield and young Jeremy Monga has been poached from Leicester.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With Rodri linked with a move away from Manchester City, Sky Sports News reporter Ben Ransom discusses whether Ayyoub Bouaddi could be brought in to replace the midfielder

The wish list also includes a right-back and a winger, while keeping tabs on Lille teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi, who excelled at the World Cup for Morocco. Arsenal are also admirers of him.

Depending on potential suitors meeting the club's valuation, outgoings might comprise a selection of: Savinho, Omar Marmoush, Nico Gonzalez, Jack Grealish, Tijjani Reijnders and Rico Lewis. Transfer activity is expected to accelerate now the World Cup has concluded.

What are Maresca's main challenges?

This is the first time since the Abu Dhabi takeover that the plan is uncertain. 10 years ago, all preparation went into building a club to lure Guardiola to the Premier League. That vision has been and gone, so where now?

City have forged a culture geared towards winning silverware, anything less is unlikely to be tolerated for a sustained period. Fans arrive at the Etihad expecting to be entertained, but above all, demanding to win. Balancing both is where Maresca's Chelsea failed.

The 46-year-old does have the benefit of not being the only managerial newbie at one of the top clubs, though, making for a changeable Premier League landscape as the natural order figures itself out. At City, that is being viewed as an opportunity to take advantage of.

Andoni Iraola at Liverpool, Xabi Alonso at Chelsea and, perhaps to a lesser extent, Michael Carrick at Man Utd, all hold question marks. This era of unknowns is fertile ground for anyone with ambition to make a mark. Very much sink or swim.

What about the 115 charges?

115 Premier League charges still cloud the club. Maresca will have to field difficult questions from the media over it.

Guardiola was the master of public-facing confrontation, having had to handle media glare at some of Europe's biggest clubs all his career. He knew the City press pack well and how to shut down any exchanges he wished not to speak on.

Maresca came under fire at Chelsea at times but mainly over football matters. How he handles this situation will likely impact his first 12 months - assuming a verdict is reached within that timeframe.

Man City have denied all of the charges.

Maresca is due to give his first Man City press conference on Friday, July 24. You can follow everything that is said in our dedicated live blog here.

Sports.title: 'Fery can improve but that's exciting' - Henman optimistic as Brit eyes US Open run
Sports.content:
British No 1 Arthur Fery will head into the American hard-court swing with areas he can improve ahead of the US Open - but that's "exciting", says Tim Henman.

The wild card's surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals has injected a much-needed shot of positivity and given British fans a new name to follow in the Grand Slams - starting at the US Open in New York - live on Sky Sports Tennis from August 30.

The challenge for the 24-year-old now is to acclimatise to his new standing in the game and the loss of anonymity and the freedom that brings with it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arthur Fery reflects on his Wimbledon experience, his massive climb up the world rankings and the tournaments he's planning to play next

The 23-year-old, who has soared to 36 in the world from No 114, was the last player standing in what was an otherwise dismal tournament for the host nation, but he became only the fifth British man this century to reach the second week at the All England Club.

Fery has earned direct entry to a Masters event for the first time in Cincinnati - 13-23 August - before appearing at the Winston-Salem Open from 23-29 August ahead of his debut at Flushing Meadows.

Speaking at Royal Birkdale ahead of The Open, Henman called Fery's dream run at the All England Club "amazing" and "transformational for his career and his life".

The former British No 1 said: "He started the year at 185 in the world, qualified in Melbourne and then has continued to improve his ranking - then getting a wild card at Wimbledon ranked 114 and winning five matches getting to the semi-finals it was an incredible performance - and I think it also shows the fine margins between these top players.

"If you're in the top 250 in the world you're an extremely good player and on your day you've got a chance of beating anyone, so huge for him to be 36 in the world now getting to the other Grand Slams and Masters 1000, so he's got an opportunity to really plan his schedule moving forward."

"I mean it's interesting that actually the ranking points will come on after Wimbledon and then the entries are six weeks out so I think the first tournament he will take advantage of that is Cincinnati," explained Henman.

Fery admits he might be plunged into the media spotlight in a similar manner to Raducanu following his fairy tale run at Wimbledon.

"Yes, even already a little bit during the tournament I was thinking of life after and how I was going to handle all that because we've seen it with people who've broken through in that manner before," Fery told Sky News' Jacquie Beltrao.

"With Emma obviously, Emma won a Slam and I didn't but there was still a lot of media attention.

"It is going to be really important to handle that - the expectation from myself and also the public."

The Brit is ready for more time in the media glare as he competes against the top players in tennis.

"It means I can play the top players week in week out and compare myself to them and keep working on my tennis," said Fery.

"I am going to have to get accustomed to the full life of tour with more media attention and all of that but I think I'm ready for it.

"It is going to be a first as well playing the US Open. I didn't even play qualifiers last year so it's going be a great experience."

"I don't think I will be able to contribute to the ranking anymore before the list comes out for the US Open, because it's going to come out soon.

"Being seeded obviously protects you a little bit from the top guys, but it's my first main draw that I qualify for directly with my ranking so just going to take it as it goes."

Sports.title: Football Daily | Here are 48 reasons to cherish the World Cup (minus the Geopolitics)
Sports.content:
MISTY, WATER-COLOURED MEMORIES

The Geopolitics World Cup is already fading from view, replaced by a thin July gruel of pre-season friendlies and transfer tales. But there’s still time to cast another look back over the 48-team, 104-game, 308-goal leviathan that has dominated the last six weeks of our lives. Without further ado, here are 48 reasons to cherish this year’s World Cup (minus the Geopolitics).

The very first game between Mexico and South Africa saw three red cards dished out, ITV showing off their studio’s Manhattan backdrop, and a duck anointed as a national hero. Germany looked ominous, putting seven past Curaçao, whose solitary goal sent Telemundo commentators wild. Vozinha and Cape Verde had us wondering about Spain, and the giant keeper’s heroics helped his mum get over to watch him play.

View image in fullscreen One more Vozinha pic for the road. Photograph: Daniel Zuchnik/Getty Images for Fanatics

Another classy veteran, Lionel Messi, banged in six group-stage goals, (briefly) becoming the World Cup’s all-time top scorer. Cristiano Ronaldo was bad, then (briefly) “back”, and then gone again. Scotland fans left a far greater impression on the tournament than their team, making Boston their spiritual home. England put away Croatia with a dazzling display of attacking intent that was not to be repeated, while Anthony Barry expertly channeled a frustrated lower-league manager in his half-time interviews.

It’s probably time for a hydration break, but Mauricio Pochettino just kicked over the Powerade. Poch did a great turn as a middle-aged actor playing a World Cup coach, and the US (briefly) looked like a really good team, before being derailed by something or other, we forget. Fellow co-hosts Canada earned their first-ever World Cup win in style, smashing six past Sunday League’s Qatar, who earned two red cards. Also sent off: discretion’s Miguel Almirón, for covering his mouth while talking – not that it helped Turkey, who crashed out after two games despite taking 1,057 shots on goal.

View image in fullscreen Miguel Almirón makes sure to let the ref see his lips. Photograph: Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters

Group E saw Japan being tidy on and off the field, an inconsistent Sweden winning and losing 5-1, and Herve Rénard showing up for some reason. Ecuador’s “touchline dreamboat” Sebastián Beccacece turned heads, while Marcelo Bielsa could only shake his dome sorrowfully as Uruguay fell apart in real time. Riyad Mahrez confused everyone by putting Algeria 3-2 up against Austria, who immediately equalised and doubled the torment for Iran, already denied a dramatic winner against Egypt by VAR.

Time for another hydro-break, brought to you by the sweet elixir of goals. Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral delivered the goal and celebration of the tournament against Argentina, who brought extra-time magic of their own thanks to Julián Alvarez. Haiti’s Wilson Isidor and Uzbekistan striker Eldor Shomurodov joined the pantheon of great forgotten World Cup goals, while Egypt’s brilliant breakaway against Argentina was cruelly disallowed. Their manager, combustible hardman Hossam Hassan, responded accordingly.

View image in fullscreen Strike! Photograph: Marco Bello/Reuters

The knockouts brought a sharper edge, with Germany bundled out by ‘housery’s Paraguay and the Dutch denied by a Morocco team who lived up to their billing. Portugal v Croatia was absolute psychodrama, and Belgium looked more likely to fight among themselves than find a way back against Senegal. The Battle of the Azteca was a belter. England players threw their heads at everything, Javier Aguirre delivered the GWC’s best touchline moment, and Harry Kane lost his voice. Brazil’s fragile, vibes-based journey was shattered by Erling Haaland’s merciless precision as Norway rowed on in (almost) perfect unison, with Haaland dominating defences and Social Media Disgraces alike. Neymar, meanwhile, won the Mark Corrigan award for winning in the most minor way possible.

On to the quarter-finals, where Kylian Mbappé dictated the play as France (briefly) looked unstoppable, and Spain conceded a goal (Charles De Ketelaere becoming an eternal pub quiz answer). Breel Embolo’s needless dive was exposed in 4K, England got a little help from on high against Norway, Gabriel Clarke stirred the pot, and Danny Murphy continued the sobering tale of Bob the Cat. The semis can be summed up in two key moments – Lamine Yamal turning Lucas Digne’s brain inside-out, and seven defenders failing to close down Enzo Fernández. Oh, England!

View image in fullscreen Lucas Digne having his blood twisted. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

The game of the tournament came in the third-place playoff, a ridiculous knockabout affair won 6-4 by England, with Mbappé stat-padding his way to the Golden Boot. The final was not nearly as much fun, with Wayne Rooney neatly summarising the chaotic half-time show, and Fernández’s bone-headed second yellow card summing up Argentina’s reductive efforts. There’s no bigger moment than the one that wins it all, though, so take a bow, Ferran Torres.

Finally, after a tournament of tedious celebrity-spotting, it was nice to see Javier Bardem and Carlos Alcaraz genuinely celebrating Spain’s success, before Keyne Yamal made the pitch his playground. Ominously, Luis de la Fuente’s red-and-gold army are co-hosts next time, when we may have to rattle off 64 memorable moments. We’ll get to work on that, you can start making your predictions and we’ll do it all again in 2030.

KEVIN KEEGAN (1951-2026)

Tributes have poured in over the last 24 hours to Kevin Keegan after his death at the age of 75. His playing career was remarkable – he remains (and will surely remain for a long time) the only British player to be twice named European Footballer of the Year, he won the title three times with Liverpool (and the European Cup), the Bundesliga with Hamburg and was an England stalwart for a decade. But through TV appearances, adverts, even a top 40 hit, his impact as one of football’s early celebrity breakout stars can’t be measured by medals alone. And that’s before we get to his wild managerial career, remembered mostly – for good or ill – by his blow-up at Alex Ferguson in 1996. “Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there’s no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players,” said Ferguson on Tuesday. “That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club too and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle – I think – their best ever team.” Amid a deluge of other tributes, Alan Shearer perhaps summed up his feelings most succinctly: “My hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.”

For more on Keegan’s remarkable career as a player and manager, here’s Rob Draper’s wonderful tribute, Richard Williams’s obituary, Louise Taylor on his three eras at Newcastle and his life in pictures.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan runs out at Anfield in August 1971 after signing for Liverpool. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result. For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn’t just about winning; it’s about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up. It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment” – despite their showing in the GWC final, Enzo Fernández hypes up Argentina’s performance without fully grasping the meaning of the words “pride” and “humility” as they return home.

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Juan Ignacio Roncoroni/EPA

RECOMMENDED FOLLOWING

Big Website: on BlueSpace, TikBook, Instachat, you name it.

double quotation mark President Trump confused (yesterday’s Football Daily)? Maybe that was down to someone telling him that Spain, who he has relentlessly criticised for not spending enough on defence, actually had the best one of all the GWC participants” – John Myles.

double quotation mark Despite your rather mixed review (yesterday’s Football Daily), I actually thought the GWC was quite good. My main focus was the Golden Boot race. Forget match quality or results. With so many elite scorers doing loads of goals it was quite intriguing to see who would come out on top. And for a wee while one of my countrymen, Elijah Just, had the impertinence to be in the mix with his three goals for New Zealand. Exciting” – Rod de Lisle.

double quotation mark So the third-place game was 90 minutes of pointless action and the final was a shot-for-shot remake of the 2010 version? How fittingly American” – Rowan Sweeney.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … John Myles. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: ‘The scrutiny is constant’: referee Anthony Taylor retires from football
Sports.content:
Anthony Taylor has announced his retirement from elite refereeing after a distinguished career spanning more than two decades and 831 matches.

One of England’s most accomplished officials, the 47-year-old officiated 668 matches in the professional game in England. He brings the curtain down on his career following his final appointment – the World Cup last-16 tie between Portugal and Spain in the United States.

Reflecting on his career, Taylor said: “Officiating at the elite level has been an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant. The time is now right to step aside and look forward to transitioning to the next chapter of my career.

“I want to express my deepest gratitude to my two assistants Gary and Adam, my refereeing colleagues and everyone connected with the game for all their support over the years. Most importantly, I want to thank my family and friends for their unwavering support throughout the immense sacrifices this career has demanded.”

Over 16 Premier League seasons, Taylor took charge of 432 top-flight matches and officiated every major domestic cup final. His honours include the FA Cup finals in 2017 and 2020, the 2015 League Cup final, the 2015 Community Shield and the 2018 Championship play-off final.

Taylor also enjoyed an outstanding international career, spending 14 years on the Fifa international list. During that time, he officiated at two World Cups (2022 and 2026), two Euros (2020 and 2024) and two Club World Cups (2022 and 2025).

Quick Guide How do I 

Across the 163 international matches he took charge of, Taylor was entrusted with some of world football’s biggest fixtures, including the 2020 Uefa Super Cup, the 2021 Nations League final, the 2022 Club World Cup final, the 2023 Europa League final and the 2024 Champions League semi-final.

Howard Webb, chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, said: “Anthony has been a fantastic servant to the game over many years, both domestically and on the international stage. He has been repeatedly trusted to officiate in the biggest games including Portugal against Spain in this summer’s World Cup which ultimately capped off an outstanding career.

“He’s consistently demonstrated over a sustained period why he is one of the best and most successful officials that English football has ever produced, but it’s not just his on-field achievements that see him as a role model to many. The professionalism he’s shown and the support for his colleagues and the next generation of officials looking to follow in his footsteps is testament to his character.

“We thank him for his immense contribution to the game and wish him every success in the next chapter of his career.”

Sports.title: La Liga chief claims Fifa is ‘destroying football industry’ and calls for Infantino to quit
Sports.content:
La Liga’s president, Javier Tebas, has accused Fifa of “destroying the football industry” and called for its president, Gianni Infantino, to quit. Tebas spoke out as the dust settled on the 2026 World Cup with suggestions that the 2030 tournament could be increased from 48 to 64 teams.

“Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense,” Tebas said in an interview with the Italian newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport. “The football industry is not just the World Cup, which is the most important event. Not everything can revolve around the World Cup. It is national competitions that support this sport.

“They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players. We need fewer national teams and more protection for national football, at all levels. They don’t realise, they are making irresponsible decisions.”

Tebas said Infantino should leave his position. “His time is up. However, he has the support of the system, of the federations, so there is not much more to add, is there?

“There is no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it is a system rotten at its core.

“These past few days here in America I have heard many people who are against Infantino, who disagree with what he does. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don’t know if silence or complicity is worse, because those who are silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering.”

Infantino has been a controversial figure during his 10 years as Fifa president. He is poised to be re-elected for a fourth term in Fifa’s March 2027 congress, although Tebas believes Infantino might have been brought down by the Folarin Balogun affair if the USA had beaten Belgium in their World Cup last-16 tie.

Scandal-proof: why Infantino's Fifa power can't be touched – video

The USA striker’s one-match ban was suspended by Fifa’s disciplinary committee, allowing him to play against Belgium, after a phone call to Infantino from Donald Trump. Infantino said the decision to revoke Balogun’s ban was taken independently by the disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Tebas said: “The suspension of the American player’s ban was absolutely serious; they were lucky Belgium eliminated the USA because a case could have arisen that might have cost Infantino his job. Since Belgium won, they managed to bury the matter.

“But these things are just the tip of the iceberg. Fifa arranges things as it wants, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football. So, if they need a 27-minute half-time break, they’ll have it.

“Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but when it’s genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, Atlanta had air conditioning; I had to put on a jumper in the stands. It was a lie, a break for advertising.”

Fifa has been approached for comment.

Sports.title: In the US, the 2026 World Cup’s legacy will be an invitation to do it all again | Leander Schaerlaeckens
Sports.content:
You do not, under any circumstance, have to hand it to Fifa.

You do, however, have to acknowledge that the 2026 World Cup was successful in all of the ways it was intended to be successful. The soccer was interesting and competitive and dramatic, albeit mostly not great – not that this really a necessary ingredient for a compelling sporting product. People came and watched in overwhelming numbers. There was fun and folklore; underdog surprises; heroic storylines that might have been hackneyed had they been works of fiction. The whole thing made vast sums of money for its organizer. More money, by an order of billions, than even Fifa itself had projected, per the Guardian’s reporting.

The tournament even went some way towards normalizing the controversial and mandatory hydration breaks, whether needed or not. This time around, we booed; next time, we’ll shrug. And while Fifa claims that it made no additional revenue from these glorified commercial breaks – the way Fox Sports chose to fill them in the United States, at any rate – you can be absolutely certain that the value created for broadcasters will be brought up in the next round of rights negotiations.

The expanded field of 48 teams worked out fine, as the worst teams were, by and large, not the debutants. So fine, in fact, that a further bloating to 64 teams is now, in a growing number of rooms filled with sportocrats, evidently being talked about less as a fringe idea by heretics than as a not-unreasonable and even natural next step.

In the end, it was all there. All of it happened the way it was supposed to.

This fully Americanized World Cup took a great deal from the United States – the countdowns; the half-time show; the championship rings; the commercial breaks; the “let’s get ready to rumble” guy telling us to get ready to rumble; not starting either half of the final on time; the dynamic pricing; and more.

But what did it give? What did it leave behind?

Not all that long ago, Fifa still insisted the World Cup was about spreading the sport, conquering new lands, evangelizing in the emerging territories. Will a boring and quarrelsome final have a tail long enough for any sort of momentum to affix itself to it? Will we remember it at all in a few years? What will soccer look like in North American now that all is said and done?

This is a three-pronged question. Mexico hosted the thing for a third time and will be broadly pleased with how it went. El Tri finally made it to the elusive “fifth game”, but nevertheless stranded at the same stage – the last 16 – they did at every World Cup from 1994 through 2018.

Canada, who stood to gain or lose the most as the only first-time hosts, scaled new heights on the field and nevertheless felt good about what they had shown when they were trounced 3-0 by Morocco. The country had, after all, put on a series of good parties that its guests will long remember.

And what of the United States? The legacy of the tournament may prove complicated here. The games were exclusive and inaccessible. And Fifa structured the thing in such a way that every penny of its mammoth haul will first head back to Switzerland. There will be no pot of money left over from the tournament for local organizers to reinvest up and down the game, the way there was in 1994. The US Soccer Federation was largely marginalized, in fact, and left to work around the edges in hopes of actually accomplishing something lasting and meaningful at the grassroots level.

Did soccer make new fans? Probably not very many in the stadiums, since it’s doubtful that any significant number of people will have dropped several thousand dollars on a lark, hoping they might have a good time at this sport they’re just getting into. Certainly, the TV ratings suggest a raft of new viewers tuned in, but did they catch the soccer bug? It will be some years before we really know.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk: World Cup Edition Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

1:30 World Cup 2026 in 90 seconds: a photo animation with audio

Besides, soccer did not, and does not, have a popularity problem in the United States. It was already on a steep ascent. Certainly, any and all converts will be welcomed into the tent. But the global game was already very much a part of the American fabric.

What soccer in the US has is an access problem. Access to a recreational youth game that hasn’t been devoured by the hypercapitalist, pay-to-play travel scene. Access, for those who do have talent and ambition, to the right coaches at the right ages, who prioritize development over winning. Access to fields and equipment and fresh air and a good old run-around.

Will this World Cup help with any of those issues?

As far as Fifa is concerned, this edition offered proof of concept. That it can expand without penalty. That it can get away with price-gouging, and that it will be rewarded enormously for it. That it will get away with all the extra contrivances and perversions and embellishments it can conjure up.

By the same mechanism that allowed Gianni Infantino to engineer a 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia, a return to the US in 2038 seems a strong possibility. There is talk, too, of hosting the Fifa Club World Cup in the US again in 2029, same as in 2025. A 2031 Women’s World Cup co-hosted here is all but a done deal.

That, in the end, may be what Fifa has built here: a colony.

Sports.title: ‘The utmost respect for him’: Alex Ferguson pays tribute to Kevin Keegan
Sports.content:
Sir Alex Ferguson has saluted Kevin Keegan for building Newcastle’s “greatest team”. Keegan, who had cancer, died on Monday at the age of 75 and Ferguson has joined the tributes for one of football’s most endearing characters.

Ferguson and Keegan were involved a fierce battle for Premier League supremacy, with Ferguson’s Manchester United pipping Newcastle to the title in 1996. “I had the utmost respect for him,” Ferguson told Track Radio. “We had many duels when he was manager of Newcastle, but the job he did at Newcastle was fantastic. He re-energised that club and he brought that enthusiasm and fanaticism great supporters can give.

“And he also brought three great players to the club – [David] Ginola, [Faustino] Asprilla, Philippe Albert – and added a bit of class to the team. The challenges we had with Newcastle at that time were huge.”

Keegan, frustrated by Ferguson’s comments in the media towards the end of the tense title fight, memorably ranted at the Scot in a television interview. Despite that, Ferguson remained friendly with the former Liverpool and England striker and admired Keegan’s impressive rebuilding job at Newcastle.

The club were in danger of relegation to the third tier when Keegan took over, but he saved them from that fate and then won promotion to the Premier League in 1993. Keegan made Newcastle so dynamic they were referred to as “the entertainers”.

Ferguson believes the title runners-up were the best team in the club’s history. “Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there’s no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players,” he said. “That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle – I think – their best ever team.”

View image in fullscreen Tributes at St James’ Park for Kevin Keegan, who died on Monday. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

Ferguson said he and Keegan had bumped into each other at a pub near Wentworth golf club a few weeks after that season. They spent the night around a piano with all thoughts of the rivalry forgotten. “The great thing about him, he held no grudges,” Ferguson said. “That was a fantastic quality he had and we had a great night.

“All aside whatever happened in previous weeks, that was soon forgotten. I really respected him for that.”

Sports.title: Neuer to Neymar: 11 World Cup players who retired from international football
Sports.content:
Manuel Neuer (Germany, 40)

First participated in the World Cup in 2010 before winning the trophy four years later. Germany have had little success since and their penalty shootout defeat by Paraguay marked the end of Neuer’s international career. He initially retired after Euro 2024 but reversed that decision a few weeks before this tournament. “Despite the bitter end, I don’t regret this decision,” he said after his 23rd and final World Cup appearance. The former Germany defender Robert Huth criticised the decision to bring Neuer out of retirement: “I think the big one that really unsettles the squad was the Neuer inclusion. I think [it was] really unexpected, he came late to the table.”

Patrik Schick (Czechia, 30)

Made his World Cup debut this summer having left an impression at Euro 2020. Schick failed to score as Czechia went winless and were eliminated in the group stage. The striker announced his international retirement hours after the final group game. “Today, my national team chapter is coming to an end,” he said. The official Czechia statement paid tribute: “Thank you for every match, every goal, and the pride with which you represented the Czech Republic.”

Guillermo Ochoa (Mexico, 41)

Cemented himself as a fans’ favourite in 2014 when he kept a famous clean sheet against the World Cup hosts, Brazil. His playing time was limited this summer, but he got 12 minutes against Czechia, where he was celebrated by teammates. After full time the manager, Javier Aguirre, said: “The moment he stepped on to the pitch, it overshadowed everything else. He is a world-class legend, and I am incredibly proud of him.” Ochoa later posted: “It was the greatest privilege of my life. Thank you for believing, for always accompanying us. I love you Mexico.”

View image in fullscreen Guillermo Ochoa shows his emotions after Mexico’s exit against England. Photograph: Álex Cruz/EPA

Riyad Mahrez (Algeria, 35)

Having made one appearance at the 2014 finals, Mahrez had to wait 12 years to add to his tally. He scored two goals against Austria before Algeria were eliminated in the last 32 by Switzerland in his final game. Mahrez said: “Representing Algeria has been a dream of mine ever since I was young, to play for my country. It’s been an immense honour and a great source of pride.” A Confederation of African Football’s statement said: “You gave us memories that time can never take away. Thank you, Riyad Mahrez.”

Enner Valencia (Ecuador, 36)

The forward got six goals in as many matches across the 2014 and 2022 finals but was unable to add to that tally for an Ecuador team who lost to Mexico in the last 32. “I’ve played my last match with the national team,” he said in the tunnel after. Ecuador’s official X account showed appreciation to their record scorer: “The GOAT. Super Enner. Thank you for giving yourself to the country and representing it in the best way.”

Nicolás Otamendi (Argentina, 38)

The uncompromising defender played every minute as Argentina triumphed in Qatar, having made his World Cup debut in 2010. Playing time was harder to come by in North America, though he featured in every game bar one, having revealed his intention to retire in March. “It’s my last World Cup, from there I’ll be a fan,” he said. Otamendi’s final home match became a tribute, with Lionel Messi letting him score a penalty at La Bombonera.

Marko Arnautovic (Austria, 37)

This was the striker’s first and last World Cup. He scored twice as Austria reached the last 32, where they were defeated 3–0 by Spain. Arnautovic revealed his departure in an emotional post-match interview, saying: “Playing for Austria was the biggest highlight. It hits me that from now on I won’t see my second family any more.” In a social media post, the Austrian Football Association said: “What a career. What a character. Thank you for everything.”

Sadio Mané (Senegal, 34)

Participated in 2018 but injury ruled him out four years later. Following Senegal’s capitulation against Belgium, Mané released a statement regarding retirement via Senegalese outlet Le Quotidien – although there have been questions about its authenticity – saying: “Know that I sacrificed everything for this flag. I gave the very best of myself and I always fought fiercely for our homeland.” Pape Thiaw was asked about Mané’s retirement in January and replied: “We want to keep him as long as possible … when we say it’s his decision, it doesn’t just belong to him, he belongs to the people of Senegal, and they want to see him carry on.”

View image in fullscreen Sadio Mané has called time on his international career with Senegal. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/FIFA/Getty Images

Craig Gordon (Scotland, 43)

The goalkeeper amassed 84 caps, making his debut in 2004, but did not get off the bench at his first World Cup. “I’ve never wanted it to end, but it must,” Gordon said, calling time on his club and international career. Gordon’s spell was described as “a career unlike any other” by the Scotland national team’s social media account.

Jean Michaël Seri (Côte d’Ivoire, 35)

Made his World Cup debut in his side’s 2–0 victory over Curaçao, his 64th cap. In a social media post, the former Fulham midfielder later said: “After 11 years in the national team, and one World Cup played, I announce the end of my international career today.” Seri received a wealth of tributes below his post. “Congratulations on all that you’ve accomplished with the national team,” replied the captain, Franck Kessié. “Thank you for all these moments shared under our colors.”

Neymar (Brazil, 34)

Announced himself on the World Cup stage with two goals on debut in 2014. Restricted by injury at the current tournament, he managed 55 minutes before Brazil’s exit against Norway and announced his international retirement shortly after full time. “It started here at MetLife Stadium,” he said, referring to his debut against the US in August 2010, “and I finished here. It is now over.” Zlatan Ibrahimovic, working as a pundit for US television, said: “An amazing player, and the skill set he had was just crazy. So, sad moment for Brazilian football.”

Sports.title: Spurs break their women’s transfer record to sign Alice Sombath from Lyonnes
Sports.content:
Tottenham have signed the France defender Alice Sombath from Lyonnes for a club record fee. The price paid for the 22-year-old has not been disclosed but the previous club record, paid for Signe Gaupset in January, was reportedly more than £375,000.

“The league is very competitive, every game is a tough game and that’s what I’m most excited about,” said Sombath. “I saw that Spurs had a very good season last year. My qualities can bring something to the team, even though I know they already have a lot.”

Sombath spent six years at Lyonnes, the eight-time European champions, joining the club after she was signed from Paris Saint-Germain in 2020.

She won the Champions League in her second season, featuring twice and being on the bench in the final, and won five league titles and two Coupe de France titles.

Tottenham’s head coach, Martin Ho, said the defender “fits the profile of what we’re building”. She has already shown real maturity in her performances and we believe she has all the qualities to continue developing into a top player within our environment.

“Alice is an aggressive defender who is comfortable in possession, competitive in her duels and has the ambition to keep improving every day. Those characteristics are really important to us and we’re excited to help her take the next step in her career while strengthening the squad.”

Sombath is Spurs’s sixth signing of the summer, after Shekiera Martinez, Kirsty Hanson, Victoria Pelova, Caitlin Dijkstra and Selma Panengstuen.

The club are delighted to have got these deals done early, allowing for a full pre-season, and that Sombath’s recruitment means they have secured the services of their six priority targets.

Sports.title: Liverpool could become worth $6billion as club enters talks with consortium backed by Mittal family
Sports.content:
Liverpool could become worth $6billion as club enters talks with consortium backed by Mittal family

A consortium backed by the Mittal family are in talks with Liverpool to buy a minority stake in the club, talkSPORT understands.

Negotiations are happening between the Reds and the consortium led by Amit Bhatia, but nothing is finalised at this stage.



2 Liverpool could be become worth more than $6billion if deal is completed Credit: Getty

Bhatia, who left his position as director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers on Tuesday, is the son-in-law of billionaire Lakshmi Mittal.

Liverpool's owners, Fenway Sports Group, have confirmed that they have been approached in a statement to the Financial Times.

It reads: “An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club."



The club is expected to be valued at more than $6billion in any transaction, which is one of the highest valuations ever.

It is reported that Bhatia has hired advisers to work on an offer amid the negotiations with current owners FSG.



However, he has yet to comment on the ongoing talks.

Freeing up for a new investment

As mentioned, Bhatia departed QPR on Tuesday by transferring his ownership to majority owner Ruben Gnanalingam.

He is said to have done this to avoid holding a stake in two clubs, which owners are not allowed to do in English football.



Speaking after his exit, Bhatia said: “Since joining the club in 2007, QPR has been a deeply important part of my life, and of my family’s life. Over nearly two decades we have shared promotions, relegations, unforgettable highs and painful lows, and the memories we have made at Loftus Road alongside the supporters will stay with us forever.

“I step back from my formal responsibilities with pride, gratitude and affection. I want to thank the players, managers, staff, the Community Trust, my fellow board members and, above all, the fans, who have made me and my family feel part of the QPR family for so many years."

Who are the Mittal family?

Lakshmi Mittal is the executive chairman of ArcelorMittal, who are the world's second-biggest steelmaking company.

He is also the chairman of stainless steel manufacturer Aperam.

The Mittal family are also involved in Indian Premier League cricket side Rajasthan Royals, holding a 75 per cent stake.



They also have a three per cent stake in QPR.

Bhatia is married to Lakshmi's daughter Vanisha Mittal.

And the family are now working on a deal to acquire a stake in Liverpool and make it one of the highest-valued clubs.

2 Mittal is a billionaire who has made his money in the steel industry Credit: Getty

Sports.title: FBI Director opens up on scale of World Cup protection brief, ’78 Super Bowls in 38 days’
Sports.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel likened the FBI's security throughout the World Cup as being like securing 78 Super Bowls in a month-and-a-half.

FBI Director opens up on scale of World Cup protection brief, ’78 Super Bowls in 38 days’

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had its work cut out through the 2026 World Cup.

With 104 football matches taking place across the United States, Canada, and Mexico over the course of 38 days, the World Cup was classed by the FBI as Special Event Assessment Rating Level One (SEAR One).

4 Spain won the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty

This is the same classification as the NFL's Super Bowl and MLB World Series, which means that, by law, the Department of Homeland Security is required to provide support for them.

For FBI Director Kash Patel, the first World Cup in 32 years to take place on American soil meant the task of providing security for the World Cup was the equivalent to 78 Super Bowls in just over a month.

"That’s what we executed on," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital

"We’re proud to report that, thank God, and thankfully to the men and women of the FBI and our partners, we had no significant criminal attacks during this World Cup.

"And just to put that in perspective, we had 6.5 million people attend the 78 matches in the U.S. across 11 venues."

Attendance figures were shattered with an estimated seven million fans travelling to watch football's spectacle.

There were also more games than ever before due to the tournament's expansion from 32 to 48 teams.

The FBI reportedly dedicated almost 5,000 personnel to their security efforts, of which over 4,000 came from field offices, 800 from FBI headquarters and further support from 59 Homeland Security task forces.

A huge part of their operations was to shut down the increase in drone threats, with the FBI revealing that they had seized over 700 drones ahead of the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, detecting over 1,600 in total.

"If you’re in the space, we’re gonna take you down. And that’s why we took down over 700," Patel stated.

4 FBI director Kash Patel likened the World Cup to being like providing security for '78 Super Bowls in 38 days' Credit: Getty

4 The FBI seized over 700 illegal drones during the World Cup Credit: AFP

"Some of these folks were maybe borderline nuisances, while many of them were criminal in terms of violations of FAA airspace and also failing to register their drones… We’re not taking any chances.

"We, the FBI, specifically train for the worst of the worst," Patel added, referring to the potential threat of drones being packed with explosives or chemical agents.

This risk of threat was heightened when four men conspired in a targeted attack on the south lawn of the White House using drones at the 'Freedom 250' UFC event back in June.

Patel praises Trump for his role

But the operation for the World Cup also required assistance internationally, assembling a Joint Operations Center with foreign representatives from 46 of the 48 participating countries at the World Cup.

"They’re working overseas in their home locations and giving us information back in real time on any single threat that’s coming in," Patel said.

In his interview with Fox News, Patel also thanked US President Donald Trump for his role in assembling the White House Task Force, spearheaded by Andrew Giuliani.

4 Patel praised Trump for assembling the White House's World Cup task force Credit: AFP

"Like anything in government, to succeed, you need tremendous leadership," Patel said.

"President Trump had the foresight to establish the White House Task Force… and what they were able to do was bring in the interagency, at least at the federal level, and then work with us at the state and local levels through our partnerships and put everybody under one roof. ...

"President Trump set the standard: Not only were we going to have the largest and safest sporting event in the history of the world, but we were going to make sure everyone had a great time. Those were the marching orders," Patel said.

"They wanted not just safety and security, but to show off America to the world. And I think we did it brilliantly."

Trump has already been vocal about wanting to hold the World Cup again, although as the sole host, and not with Canada or Mexico.

The earliest time they would be able to host again would be 2038, with the 2030 edition taking place across World Cup winners Spain, Portugal and Morocco, while the 2034 tournament is due to be held in Saudi Arabia.
