World.title: Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
World.content:
Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

toggle caption Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Monday imposed 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, declaring that Canada has unfairly discriminated against American autos, alcohol and dairy products.

The move could unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump's return to the White House. The administration official previewing the action said that Canada was one of the only nations other than China that retaliated against Trump's previous tariffs and must be held accountable.

The official insisted on anonymity on a call with reporters to preview the president's actions and said that Trump signed three proclamations to launch the tariffs under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section because they said Trump could use it to destabilize the economy.

Sponsor Message

The new 50% tariffs would exclude energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals, but they would include goods that had previously been protected from import taxes by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. That 2020 trade pact was not renewed by the U.S., triggering a new set of negotiations that could run until 2036.

The White House said in a fact sheet that the tariffs would go into effect in 30 days, meaning there is time for negotiations as Trump has not always followed through on his announced tax hikes on imports.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that his government believes in the "benefits of free and fair trade," having signed "more than 20 new economic and security partnerships." He said Canada is prepared to negotiate with the Trump administration.

"This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the U.S.," Carney said. "Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the U.S. to the mutual benefit of our citizens."

Canada faces the risk of a broader trade war

Still, the tariffs could escalate into a wider trade war as Canada seeks to defend its economy. Ontario Premier Doug Ford saw a possible showdown ahead.

Sponsor Message

"If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," Ford posted on social media.

Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, said the Trump administration's moves were "regrettable" but the two countries need to use the 30-day window before the tariffs start "to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks."

Chris Swonger, CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, also called for a deal: "We encourage policymakers on both sides of the border to pursue a negotiated solution that restores market access for U.S. spirits and avoids further harm to the U.S. hospitality sector."

But the use of a Great Depression-era law to impose the tariffs broadens some of the risks, as those tariffs could be applied to other U.S. trading partners, not just Canada, and inject "massive uncertainty" into the global economy, said Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

"We crossed the Rubicon," Lincicome said. "The invocation of 338 is the nuclear option for Trump tariffs."

Tariffs are also a political challenge for Trump

The new tariffs carry serious political and economic risks for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections for control of Congress. His "Liberation Day" tariffs last year in April provoked a financial market meltdown over concerns about inflation and a recession, prompting him to walk back the rates for a period of negotiation.

The Supreme Court ruled this February that Trump had lacked the legal authority to impose the tariffs by declaring an economic emergency, causing the administration to find alternative ways to raise import taxes based on a series of legal authorities.

Tariffs are taxes on imports, which companies can then pass along to consumers in the form of higher prices. The president maintains that the costs created by tariffs will cause manufacturing to relocate to the U.S., though there is little evidence of that in the economic data.

Sponsor Message

"These new taxes will raise prices on American families and likely lead to retaliation against the very industries Trump purportedly wants to protect," said Rep. Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., who is chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

The latest import taxes could worsen Trump's weak ratings on the economy. He promised voters when running for the presidency that he would bring prices down, but the annual inflation rate has risen since he became president because the tariffs and the war in Iran are pushing up oil prices.

Trump has repeatedly targeted Canada on trade issues

The Trump administration official said the president had also requested that his aides look into additional tariffs on Canada because its wildfires hurt air quality in the U.S. He had publicly threatened to do so in social media posts.

At the World Cup final on Sunday, Trump watched the game with Carney. The Trump administration official said their time together at the game was not a working visit to discuss trade and tariffs.

Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the U.S. president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.

Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25% tariff on the imports of U.S. motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA.

The White House said that, regarding alcohol, all but two Canadian provinces and territories halted the purchase and retailing of American alcoholic beverages beginning last year, which was also a response to Trump's tariffs and taunts of making Canada the 51st state.

But Trump has long objected to Canada's treatment of U.S. cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the U.S. compared to Europe on dairy products.

Sponsor Message

Trump and Carney have had a frosty relationship, with Carney, a former central banker, who pledged to go "elbows up" for Canada during his election campaign last year.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, Carney called out Trump — without naming him — by saying that the "most powerful" countries are using the economy to coerce less powerful nations.

Trump responded at the time by saying: "Canada lives because of the United States."

World.title: The best economic ideas from around the world — Planet Money Summer School is back
World.content:
The best economic ideas from around the world — Planet Money Summer School is back

NPR

Sweeter than ice cream, more useful than sunscreen, better than a day at the beach: Planet Money Summer School is back!

This year, Planet Money Summer School is taking your brain on a world tour in search of the best economic ideas to bring home. For more than 15 years, we've packed up our microphones and traveled the globe in search of people and stories that explain how the economy really works. We're really proud to be one of the few podcasts that get out and do this for economics stories. So, this summer, we're revisiting some of our favorite places, people, and reporting — and pairing those stories with new conversations with the economists best suited to unpack the big ideas behind them.

Sponsor Message

(You can listen to past seasons of Planet Money Summer School here. We've covered economic history, investing, and the basics of micro- and macroeconomics among other topics.)

Episodes drop every Wednesday until Labor Day in the Planet Money podcast feed.

In Episode 1, we see how Australia used a market to help put scarce water resources to their "best" uses. But at the same time, it invited speculators to profit from water. So who wins? Then, we meet the New Zealand economist — who is also a jazz musician — who invented one of the most influential ideas in modern central banking: inflation targeting.

In future episodes, we'll head to Norway to learn how a nation can beat the paradox of plenty (aka the resource curse) to get rich and stay rich, while selling its surplus resources to the rest of the world. In China, we see what happens when you run an economy like an engineer, and the perils of overbuilding.

NPR

Everywhere we stop, we are collecting innovative ideas worth borrowing (or avoiding). By the end of the series in late August, we probably won't have all of the world's problems solved. But we do hope to have assembled enough good ideas for a few good conversations — or maybe even a few ideas worth pestering your elected representatives about.

Sponsor Message

Thanks to everyone who's sent us ideas so far. Timothy, who lived in Taiwan, told us he was struck by how simple filing taxes was there.

"You simply used a downloadable program provided by the government to complete your taxes — no complex loopholes, deductions, etc," he writes. "It took me maybe 30 minutes to complete it."

Timothy says he'd love it if the U.S. adopted something similar. "I know the lucrative tax prep industry would loudly oppose this," he writes, "but their accountants could find new jobs."

Kate writes about informal savings groups known as ROSCAs (Rotating Savings and Credit Associations). "They're everywhere, from West Africa to Latin America and parts of Asia, and millions of people rely on them instead of banks," she writes. "At first glance they seem irrational. Why would you hand your money to a group when you could just save it yourself? But once you dig in, they become a fascinating story about economics, trust, commitment devices, social capital, and financial inclusion."

What's the most interesting economic idea you've encountered while traveling or living abroad?

Send us your ideas: planetmoney@npr.org. Put "Summer School" in the subject line. We'll feature some of our favorite submissions in our final episode.

World.title: How soccer brings a Bhutanese community together in Harrisburg, Pa.
World.content:
How soccer brings a Bhutanese community together in Harrisburg, Pa.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

HARRISBURG, Pa. — At a park in the hills of central Pennsylvania, children in jerseys shout in a mix of English and Nepali, chasing a ball across the grass while their parents watch from the sidelines. A mother cheers on her son. For this community of Nepali-speaking Bhutanese refugees, the field is more than a field. It's where they've rebuilt a homeland that no longer exists.

Tens of thousands of Bhutanese refugees settled in Harrisburg starting in the late 2000s, after their families were forced out of Bhutan in an ethnic-cleansing campaign on the Lhotshampa people, as the country sought to modernize and unify and the government enacted policies in the 1980s that targeted ethnic Nepalis' legal status and culture. The refugees spent nearly two decades in camps in Nepal. It was there that soccer became a lifeline. Barred from work permits, families built farms and schools by day. At night, they turned to the sport to help cope with their traumas. One refugee, Kalu Singh Tamang, had been a national soccer star in Bhutan before the expulsion. In the Beldangi camps of Jhapa, Nepal, he coached thousands of fellow refugees on how to play. He died in the camp, never getting the chance to leave.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

That tradition crossed the ocean with the community that carried it. In 2007, the U.S., with the support of the U.N., initiated a program that resettled about 85,000 refugees. Each year, a memorial tournament bearing Tamang's name reunites refugees from across the country. Birkha Gurung, one of its co-founders, said he started it because, "When we were in Nepal, in the refugee camp, I played with [Tamang] and he coached so many of the refugee soccer fans. Our community, especially the adults, are having so many problems with mental health issues [since the camps], so I started this adults' tournament." Proceeds now fund Soccer for Success, a youth program serving over 50 kids a week — passing the game down to children who might never see the camps or the country their parents fled.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

Both programs run through Asian Refugees United (ARU), a Harrisburg nonprofit that also teaches cultural classes to refugee children. But the fields have become something else too: one of the few places this community still feels safe, as it faces a wave of deportations unlike anything it has seen before.

Sponsor Message

Under an intensified immigration crackdown, dozens of community members have been deported over the last 18 months. Before March 2025, the U.S. government did not deport these stateless refugees regardless of criminal history. Now they are being flown to Bhutan — a country that still refuses to recognize them as citizens and expels them on arrival to India or Nepal. Unable to repatriate to Bhutan, Nepal, or the U.S., they are left stateless twice over, with nowhere left to land.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to requests for comment.

ARU co-founder Robin Gurung has traded running soccer programs for full-time advocacy, spending evenings and weekends with immigration attorneys, training staff in civic engagement, and flying to Washington to meet lawmakers. "We were not prepared for this when we [built] the rapid response team. Our job now requires us to talk to the family members, folks who are in ICE detention. The immediate need is to stop the deportations. Folks who are deported, they are not safe," Gurung said.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

The fear has outrun the deportations themselves. Bhagawat Dulal, a Soccer for Success coach who now also translates for detainees, said even ordinary life has started to feel dangerous. "I had some people I was talking to ask, 'Can I go garden or should I not do that because of the [ICE] situation?' The one thing that has always been there through Bhutan, Nepal and to America: We found a way to garden, because that is what brought us joy — and now the same people are scared to go garden," Dulal said. "I'm so frustrated."

Sponsor Message

Even so, the fields fill every week with children learning the game from their elders. The community still gathers to mark their religious festivals. Their trades from life before the camps are flourishing through small businesses. On the soccer field, as everywhere else, they keep carrying forward what ARU staff member Manju Gurung called, ahead of a day of advocacy on Capitol Hill, "a future of hope, for our parents and all refugee parents around the globe."

World.title: Amid U.S.-Iran war, Houthi rebels threaten to blockade another key strait
World.content:
Amid U.S.-Iran war, Houthi rebels threaten to blockade another key strait

toggle caption Mohammed Huwais/AFP via Getty Images

TEL AVIV, Israel — The Houthis, a Yemeni Shia militia that is aligned with Iran, have announced a naval blockade of a key waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

In a video statement, a Houthi spokesperson said the blockade was in retaliation for strikes from Saudi Arabia on a major airport in Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

The Houthis have accused Saudi Arabia of hitting the airport while an Iranian official was traveling through it earlier this month.

Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and it lets Saudi Arabia, one of the biggest oil producers in the world, get millions of barrels of oil a day out to the open ocean for export.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Bab el-Mandeb has become even more important for Saudi Arabia now that the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed off by the U.S.-Iran war.

Any potential Houthi blockade of the strait would rattle energy markets already shaken by the war in Iran and would likely raise energy prices further.

The blockade would also test Gulf states' resolve to counter Iran and Iran-aligned groups in the Middle East, including the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia condemned the blockade in a statement. The Houthis said in response that the Saudi kingdom is a "criminal" regime.

The Houthi rebels are designated by the U.S. State Department as a terrorist group.

Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the United Arab Emirates have been exploring the idea of building new oil pipelines or expanding existing ones to move oil overland instead of by sea, but those pipelines could take years to build.

U.S. and Iran trade fire — again

The U.S. and Iran traded fire for a 10th consecutive night of strikes Monday.

U.S. Central Command said late Monday it struck Iranian military command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and air defense systems.

Iran's state news agency IRNA said Iranian forces targeted three bases hosting U.S. military personnel and equipment in Kuwait last night.

Sponsor Message

The fighting has now reached a new intensity since the U.S. and Israel launched the war against Iran in February.

The Pentagon on Monday confirmed the identities of two service members killed by Iranian attacks in northern Jordan on Friday and said another still remains missing.

The Pentagon later disclosed a third service member was killed in Iraq.

That brings the death toll of the war in Iran to at least 17 service members killed. The Pentagon says 427 people have been injured to date. Iran's government says about 3,000 people in Iran have been killed in the war.

But a U.S. military official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, confirmed with NPR that the Defense Department has been slow-walking information on casualties.

Just this week the Pentagon spokesman admitted after questions from journalists that 100 service members have been injured in the last two weeks. He said most of them recovered quickly and went back to work.

Lebanon's president to meet Trump in the White House

A separate ceasefire between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon is still holding, despite ongoing Israeli strikes on people and sites in Lebanon that Israel claims are Hezbollah-affiliated.

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun is scheduled to meet President Trump in Washington on Tuesday, the first official White House visit by a Lebanese president since 2009.

His visit comes at a critical time. A sweeping roadmap for peace between Lebanon's government and Israel signed in June would see the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah. But that is preconditioned on Israel withdrawing from the large amount of Lebanese territory it has occupied since earlier this year.

So far, the timeline for any Israeli withdrawal has been unclear, and about 400,000 Lebanese people remain internally displaced because of Israeli occupation or destruction of their homes.

NPR's Quil Lawrence contributed reporting.

World.title: Amid nurse shortage, a university rolls out the welcome mat for men
World.content:
Amid nurse shortage, a university rolls out the welcome mat for men

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter sent every weekday morning.

Men are largely missing out on one of the hottest professions in the U.S. right now: nursing.

For registered nurses alone, the Labor Department projects there will be 189,000 job openings each year for the next decade. But only 1 in 8 nurses are men.

There have long been efforts to rewrite the script around nursing — to push back on the idea that it's women's work. Now, the economy is helping, too.

Sponsor Message

With diminishing opportunities in male-dominated industries like manufacturing and software engineering, nursing has emerged as a stable alternative and a solid pathway to a middle-class life.

Nursing students at the University of Alabama at Birmingham are already experiencing what it's like to be in demand.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Ethan Stinson will graduate next month and go straight into a job in the psychiatric unit at the university hospital.

"I feel like it's really easy to get a psych job if you're a nurse," he says. "They're hunting people all the time."

His classmate Hatim Nasser, whose family had wanted him to study computer science, has a job lined up in the university hospital's heart and lung transplant intensive care unit.

At a time when many of their peers are unsure of what's next, the students are happy their skills are in demand.

"We're grateful for it," Nasser says.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

A nursing school in the South leads the way

No doubt, stereotypes about men in nursing still abound. But slowly, they're being eroded.

At the University of Alabama at Birmingham, close to 1 in 6 nursing students are men, outpacing the national average. And nearly 1 in 5 faculty are men. In some specialties within the university hospital, male nurses are nearly as common as female nurses.

Sponsor Message

"I don't really feel like nursing isn't for men or anything like that. When I go to the hospital, I see guys all the time," says nursing student Amiri Saadiq, who's headed for a job in the bone marrow transplant intensive care unit.

For years, the nursing school has been intentional about creating a welcoming environment for men. It features male students on all its marketing materials. It sends male and female nurses into high schools to recruit students. There's an employee resource group for men in nursing at the university hospital.

Professor Curry Bordelon says all of this makes a difference.

"We're never going to flip the entire iceberg. But I can get one little ice cube at a time out of it," he says. "And when you do that, you're opening up that opportunity for change."

toggle caption Andi Rice//for NPR

A different landscape in the 1990s

Things were very different three decades ago when Bordelon was getting his start in what he calls "small-town Louisiana."

Men made up only 4% of nurses back then. Bordelon first learned about nursing through his aunt, who was a nurse. He was her practice patient.

Out of high school, he worked as a volunteer firefighter and found himself drawn to the medical calls.

From there, he enrolled in a nursing program at a local community college. He remembers his first day, looking around. There were about 90 students in his first class. Just three of them were men. He recalls the instructor telling the guys that the only reason they were there was to satisfy a quota.

"That, to me, was sort of a wake-up," he says. "It was a — 'I want to find my right fit where I can strive.'"

Getting help from someone who looks like you

Bordelon found a more welcoming environment at a different nursing school. Then, he found his calling: working in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), where male nurses are extremely rare.

Sponsor Message

He says fathers in the NICU would sometimes get defensive when they saw him talking to their wives about breastfeeding. But he made a point to include them, too.

"'I'm here to support the entire family unit,'" he says he would tell them. "'Which means — Dad, would you like to do skin-to-skin?'"

That simple action — holding a baby to one's bare chest — is incredibly important for the baby's long-term success, Bordelon says. Not to mention, it prepares fathers for the transition home.

Bordelon is certain that having more male nurses everywhere could improve health outcomes. Studies have found that patients respond better to healthcare providers who look like them.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Nursing student Nicholas Seay, who is Black, has already experienced this during his clinical rotations. He finds older Black men often look relieved when he walks into the room. At times, they seem more at ease talking with him than with the nurse he's shadowing.

"I think they're happy to see [a] familiar face," he says.

Seay has also experienced the opposite: female patients who are not comfortable with him at their bedside. In those situations, he steps aside.

"If I was a woman, I don't know if I'd want a male student in the room either, so I really can't be mad," he says.

"Permission" to be in nursing

Even in the cocoon of the university setting, stereotypes persist.

For one, male nurses are often mistaken for doctors. Chris Jones, a graduate student pursuing a dual master's degree in nursing and business administration, says it happens when he enters patients' rooms, as well as elsewhere in the hospital.

"They would give me the resident discount in the cafeteria, and it's a good discount," he says with a laugh. "I've had to correct them."

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

And because nursing requires patience and compassion — traits traditionally seen as feminine — there are people who assume all male nurses are gay.

Sponsor Message

Bordelon knows persistent stereotyping gives some men pause.

"A lot of times, men need permission to be in the nursing field," he says.

He's happy that popular shows like The Pitt depict men in all kinds of healthcare roles, including nursing. And, he says, the fact that the jobs pay well doesn't hurt. The national median wage for registered nurses tops $90,000 a year.

Jones, who was the first in his family to go to college, says one reason he became a nurse was so that he'd be able to take care of himself.

"And if I wanted to start a family one day, too, that I could do that as well," he says.

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

In recent years, nursing has become more technologically advanced, another draw for men, says Steven Parsons, a cardiovascular operating room nurse and adjunct instructor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

Robots are frequently used in lung surgery and sometimes in heart surgery, he says. A robotics team that he was a part of was majority male.

"You've got guys that are kind of interested in that mechanical stuff," he says.

Still, for others, the motivation for going into nursing is personal. Connor Aderholt, a former college baseball player, says he and his brother both decided to pursue careers in nursing after observing the compassionate care their grandmother received after a stroke.

"In that vulnerable moment — in our family's vulnerable moment — it made me realize, this is what I want to do, to deal with these tough situations that people have to deal with," says Aderholt. "To be that calm in the storm for other people."

toggle caption Andi Rice for NPR

Moving the needle faster

This fall, Bordelon will assume leadership of the American Association for Men in Nursing, a national advocacy group. He knows there's still much to tackle.

"Will we ever be 100% gender neutral? I don't know that," Bordelon says. "Can we help move the needle a little faster? Sure, there's opportunities for that."

Sponsor Message

He and a colleague at Purdue University School of Nursing recently scored a big win: getting men's health officially designated as a nursing specialty. Beyond urological issues, Bordelon argues, there are many other factors that drive a shorter life expectancy for men.

"We have women's health nurse practitioners. We potentially could have men's health nurse practitioners," Bordelon says. "That's our dream. That's our goal."

World.title: Carney says he and Trump have agreed to 'intensify' trade talks in wake of 50% tariff threat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's spoken to U.S. President Donald Trump after Monday's tariffs announcement and that the two leaders have agreed to intensify trade discussions in the wake of the latest tariff threat from our southern neighbours.

"I spoke with President Trump earlier this morning. We agreed to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks and the team and myself look forward to doing that," Carney said.

The prime minister said that intensification will happen "right away" but he did not provide insight into the specifics of how his government will respond to the latest tariff threat.

"We will look at all options in terms of how we would respond if [the new tariffs] do come into effect. That's part of what we will be discussing with premiers," he said.

On Monday evening, Trump announced that his administration will be imposing tariffs of 50 per cent on a wide range of Canadian exports in 30 days' time.

The new tariffs are being imposed in response to what a senior administration official described as Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy and its discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

The White House has provided detail, in three presidential proclamations, for why each of those trade irritants are considered discriminatory to the U.S.

The alcohol irritant

The Canadian alcohol bans, where every province save Alberta and Saskatchewan has banned the sale of U.S. beer, wine and spirits, were imposed after Trump slapped earlier tariffs on the auto sector, steel, aluminum, softwood lumber and other things.

According to U.S. Census Bureau figures, the alcohol bans have resulted in a $360-million US drop in wine exports to Canada in 2025 from the previous year, along with a $150-million US drop in spirit exports.

"The Canadian provinces and territories have not instituted or maintained similar bans or restrictions on any other country since March 2025, thereby benefitting other countries at the expense of the United States," the proclamation on alcohol said.

Carney said on Tuesday that the decision to remove U.S. booze from Canadian shelves was taken by the provinces in retaliation for the U.S. tariffs on key industries in their provinces, as well as threats to Canada's sovereignty in general.

"The decision to change that, first and foremost, will be taken by the provinces themselves, each individually, and should only be taken, in my view, as part of an overall agreement, and that's what we'll work to accomplish," he said.

World.title: Trump's escalating trade war puts pressure on premiers with U.S. booze boycotts as they gather in P.E.I.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's surprise escalation in his trade war with Canada is putting renewed pressure on the premiers — most of whom have pulled American booze from liquor stores — as they gather in Charlottetown for their annual summer meeting.

The White House announced on Monday that it will impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of goods in response to what a senior administration official described as Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy and its discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

The squeeze from Canada's southern neighbour has changed the environment at the annual meeting of the premiers, highlighting the provinces' division on the issue of banning U.S. alcohol.

Every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan has stopped selling American alcohol in retaliation to his previous tariffs on things like the auto sector, steel and aluminium.

The boycotts have been seen as a bargaining chip in the ongoing trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S. and have become an irritant for the Americans as U.S. exports of wine, beer and spirits to Canada have plummeted.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is holding a virtual meeting with the premiers Tuesday afternoon, where it's likely to be discussed.

"The decision to change that, first and foremost, will be taken by the provinces themselves, each individually, and should only be taken, in my view, as part of an overall agreement, and that's what we'll work to accomplish," Carney said on Tuesday.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said he expects the federal government to at some point ask the provinces to relent on the boycotts.

"I think it's already been made in some cases. So that will be a decision each province will have to make," he said Tuesday morning. "But that ask should come from the federal government, they're at the negotiating table. They'll know the sensitivities that may present."

'Not a chance in hell' of restocking U.S. booze: Eby

But some premiers are showing no signs of backing down.

B.C. Premier David Eby said "there is not a chance in hell that U.S. alcohol is going back on the shelf" in his province.

"The one way to embolden a bully is to capitulate. And I don't think we should embolden Mr. Trump, who clearly is a bully," he said at the onset of the meetings.

WATCH | Eby says 'not a chance in hell' U.S. booze going back on B.C. shelves: Not a chance in hell' U.S. booze going back on B.C. shelves: Eby | Duration 0:43 B.C. Premier David Eby, reacting Tuesday to the latest U.S. tariff announcement, said Canada's 'integrity is intact' and reiterated his unwillingness to return U.S. alcohol to shelves after President Donald Trump's latest move to hike levies on Canadian products.

Eby said earlier that he has asked staff to contact the U.S. Embassy to have his government's statement marking the two countries' friendship removed from the U.S. 250th birthday website, adding he feels "sorry for Americans."

"This feels like an increasingly desperate and flailing approach to relationships with our country," he said.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also been vocal that he won't back down. The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is one of the largest alcohol retailers in the world.

"I'll never stop fighting to protect Ontario. If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," he posted on social media on Monday.

P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz, the host of this year's conference, said the debate over alcohol will be discussed "and how it fits into this 30-day discussion about hammering out a deal over these irritants."

P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz speaks to reporters at the Council of the Federation meeting in Charlottetown on Tuesday. (Eli J. Ridder/The Canadian Press)

Carney also told reporters that he spoke with Trump on Tuesday morning and the two leaders agreed to intensify trade talks in the coming weeks.

The new tariffs, set to come into place on Aug. 19, would apply to a variety of Canadian imports, "ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement," the official said. Energy, potash, critical minerals and fish would be exempt, but other products that until now have been allowed into the U.S. tariff-free under terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) would be hit.

This follows the White House's announcement earlier this month declining to extend CUSMA, triggering what are expected to be tough negotiations on amending the continental pact.

While the U.S. turn is expected to dominate, Lantz said there's still room to discuss other agenda items. Before Monday's bombshell news, premiers had listed health-care transfers, energy development, economic growth and the wildfires destroying swaths of northern Ontario as priorities for their meetings.

WATCH | Quebec premier says supply management 'non-negotiable' in U.S. trade talks: Quebec premier says supply management 'non-negotiable' in U.S. trade talks | Duration 1:04 Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette says she will defend Quebec's workers, including dairy farmers who sell under the supply management system that has provoked threats of 50 per cent tariffs from U.S. President Donald Trump. 'Supply management is something that is non-negotiable for me,' said Fréchette.

In 2023, the federal government, under prime minister Justin Trudeau, hiked the annual Canada Health Transfer by five per cent for five years. With the transfers reverting back to three per cent increases come March 2028, the provinces are beating the drum for more federal funding.

"It's very important that before we expand responsibilities, for example, do more on dental care or do more defence spending, that we do honour our commitments to Canadian citizens of providing quality public health care," Quebec Finance Minister Eric Girard told CBC's Power & Politics last week.

Referendums off the official agenda

The meetings also come ahead of what could be internal tests to Canadian unity.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is going ahead with a series of referendum questions in October — including whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or commence the legal process of holding a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

The question of Quebec independence has also been resurrected, with Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon promising to hold a referendum on separation if he secures a mandate in the fall provincial election. While St-Pierre Plamondon's party has been dominating in the polls over the last year, recent surveys suggest the race is tightening.

In an interview late last week, New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the referendums aren't on the official agenda, "but there are also conversations that we have around the coffee pot or as we're moving in and out of different discussions.

"We were one of the four that set Canada up and I believe very firmly in the beauty of this nation from coast to coast to coast, and New Brunswick will do whatever we can to keep our country strong and united," said Holt.

World.title: How the outbreak of an intestinal parasite in the U.S. unfolded
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Federal and state authorities in the U.S. have been investigating cases of illness from an intestinal parasite.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that contaminates food that has come into contact with human feces, such as when produce is irrigated or washed with contaminated water.

Cyclosporiasis, the infection caused by the parasite, most commonly causes diarrhea, but some people can experience other gastrointestinal symptoms and dehydration. Symptoms usually start within a week of ingesting the parasite, doctors say.

The illness usually does not spread from person to person.

As of July 20, more than 30 states have reported illnesses, with about 100 hospitalizations to date and no deaths. The true number of infections is likely much higher given that many people recover without seeking medical treatment and that there is lag between when symptoms start and reporting.

Public health officials say they are not currently investiagting any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

The parasite can stick in the nooks and crannies of berries, food scientists say. (Frannyanne/Shutterstock)

Foods imported to Canada that have been linked to the Cyclospora parasite include:

Basil.

Cilantro.

Raspberries.

Blackberries.

Mesclun lettuce.

Snow and snap peas.

Pre-packaged salad mix.

This is how the current outbreak south of the border unfolded and how Canadian health officials reacted.

May 13, 2026

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says this is when the first illnesses from the C yclospora parasite started.

June 30

Michigan state health officials say as of this date, more than 170 cases have been reported across several counties compared with around 50 cyclosporiasis cases per year typically.

July 8

The Public Health Agency of Canada says it is not investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada and tells CBCNews the parasite is not commonly found on food and is not in drinking water here.

"In the spring and summer, there is usually an increase in Cyclospora infections linked to consuming fresh fruit and vegetables imported from other countries," a spokesperson for PHAC said in an email.

July 16

The FDA and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with state and local partners, investigate a multi-state outbreak of Cyclospora illnesses linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.

WATCH | A food scientist explains Cyclospora: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Illnesses start occurring between May 13, 2026, and July 13, 2026. Michigan analyzes food exposure details from 190 of the cases of people who reported eating at Taco Bell and shared these findings with CDC.

The FDA says its traceback investigation to try to find the source converged on a single supplier of iceberg lettuce from Mexico used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill.

Meanwhile, health officials in Alberta say they're investigating an uptick in cyclosporiasis. But the province said no connection has been made between the Alberta illnesses and the American outbreak.

July 17

Taylor Farms de Mexico, which provided shredded iceberg lettuce used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill, is flagged by the FDA as a supplier. The company announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

Health officials in Quebec say that since the beginning of the year, 85 cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported, compared to 30 cases in 2025 for the same period (average of 32 cases annually between 2022 and 2025).

"As in previous years, most Quebec cases are thought to be linked to travel exposure, primarily in Mexico," a spokesperson for Quebec's Ministry of Health and Social Services said in an email.

No Quebec cases appear to be associated with the outbreak in Michigan, they said.

July 18

On July 17, the FDA said Taylor Farms de Mexico, based in Guanajuato and also known as Taylor Fresh Foods, announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

A recall notice put out by Taylor Fresh Foods includes Marketside-brand iceberg lettuce products available at Walmart in the U.S.

July 19

The FDA points to the complexity of detecting Cyclospora, saying its laboratory experts concluded a new sample of shredded lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico tested positive for Cyclospora during import examination at the U.S.-Mexico border. This ended up being a false positive, the FDA said.

July 20

On social media, FDA officials clarify there is still "overwhelming epidemiological data" supporting a large voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.

The Public Health Agency of Canada says is still not currently investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

World.title: Former Toronto police officer Derek McCormick pleads guilty in Project South investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the Toronto police officers charged in the sweeping police corruption and organized crime investigation dubbed Project South pleaded guilty to two charges Tuesday morning.

Derek McCormick entered a guilty plea for breach of trust and one count of theft under $5,000 in Ontario Court of Justice in Toronto.

The other four charges McCormick was facing — three more counts of theft under $5,000 and one count of obstruction of justice — are set to be with withdrawn.

McCormick is expected to be sentenced by Justice Jonathan Bliss later Tuesday morning.

The Crown and defence proposed a joint submission for a 10-month conditional sentence, which would include five months of house arrest and five months of a 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew.

McCormick's theft and breach of trust guilty pleas concer n the now-retired constable ste aling a cellphone that was turned in to him at the front desk of 52 division, according to an agreed statement of facts.

McCormick stole the phone for Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt, who had asked McCormick to get him burner phones, the statement said.

Officer had painkiller addiction, Crown says

Crown prosecutor Vlatko Karadzic said McCormick had a painkiller addiction and was suffering from PTSD at the time of his crimes and had been buying Percocet pills from Barnhardt.

Barnhardt is also charged in Project South and has been described as the "genesis" of the investigation. The allegations against him have not been tested in court.

Karadzic told the court there is no evidence McCormick knew how the phone he provided was used.

"He's best described as a peripheral player in this project," Karadzic said of the officer in his sentencing submissions.

McCormick was suspended without pay from Toronto police in May.

McCormick retired from Toronto police at the beginning of July, according to his lawyer, Gary Clewley.

Scope of probe grew

Project South began in June 2025 when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections officer at Toronto South Detention Centre.

While investigating that alleged conspiracy, York police discovered that Barnhardt had allegedly shared confidential information about a senior correctional officer with a civilian. Police have then accused the civilian of providing that information to others charged in the alleged murder plot.

From there, the scope of the probe grew to include other alleged police corruption tied to organized crime.

The other six current police officers and a retired constable charged in Project South are expected to make their first appearance in Superior Court of Justice on Wednesday, where prosecutors are proceeding with their cases by direct indictment.

That means the cases will skip a preliminary inquiry, typically used in criminal cases to determine whether prosecutors have enough evidence to proceed with a trial, and head directly to trial.

World.title: Toronto mayor, local councillors look to ban surveillance pricing in city
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto's mayor is introducing a motion to ban surveillance pricing for groceries and other essentials, a practice where businesses adjust what they charge customers based on their personal data .

"No one should have a different price based on who you are," Chow said at a news conference before Tuesday's executive committee meeting at city hall. "That’s just not fair."

Chow moved to direct city staff to look for all possible ways Toronto can "ban and regulate surveillance pricing that increases prices on groceries, including those sold online and delivered within the city," and report back next year.

"We will fight the rising costs of groceries and protect Torontonians from being gouged by corporate giants looking to maximize their profit on the backs of regular people," she said, adding that many Torontonians are already struggling to afford the cost of living.

Coun. Alejandra Bravo, who seconded Chow's motion, said using consumer data to maximize the profit companies can extract from each individual customer is " predatory pricing."

Premier against ban, says free market keeps costs low

Other levels of government have recently considered the issue, including Manitoba, which is currently looking at making "personalized algorithmic pricing" an unfair business practice.

Conversely, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said earlier this year that he was against banning algorithmic personalized pricing, saying he believes in a free-market, capitalist society, and competition is the best way to keep prices low.

An Ontario NDP motion to ban surveillance pricing was voted down in April, shortly after Ford's comments.

The federal NDP introduced a similarly unsuccessful motion this spring to ban the practice online and in retail stores.

Weeks later, the initial draft of the federal AI strategy, though light on details, said Canada will strengthen privacy laws to ensure "personal information is not used inappropriately, including for surveillance pricing."

World.title: A 67-year-old died in one of B.C.'s oldest and largest open water swim events. Here's what we know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. Coroners Service is investigating the death of a 67-year-old man at an open water swim event on Okanagan Lake this past weekend.

Police say the man was taking part in the Across the Lake swim event, which has been running since 1949.

In a release, West Kelowna RCMP said the man was found unresponsive in the water roughly two hours after he started the event and was taken to shore. Attempts by B.C. Ambulance crews to resuscitate him failed.

WATCH | Man dies in Okanagan Lake at open water swim event: Man drowns in Okanagan Lake during mass swimming event | Duration 1:49 Police in Kelowna say a man taking part in a mass swim died over the weekend. The event called Across the Lake Swim, attracts more than 1,000 swimmers each year on a course across Okanagan Lake.

Multiple race participants reported being blown off course by high winds and choppy waters unlike those they've experienced in past years.

About the event

Event organizers have yet to comment on the death.

According to the event's website, Across the Lake is "the largest and longest continuously running open water swim event in Canada."

Participants swim either 2.1 kilometres or 1.5 kilometres, starting in West Kelowna and ending at Hot Sands Beach in Kelowna.

The Across the Water sees participants swim either 2.1 or 1.5 kilometres across Okanagan Lake. (Across the Water)

The event includes a competitive category and open swims for all ages. Roughly 1,200 people registered for this year's competition.

Support paddlers — people in boats or paddleboards who provide support to swimmers — are allowed but are not required for participation, the website says.

Choppy waters

Many participants have reported challenging conditions that took them off course.

Tiana Langedyk said she was among those pulled off course as winds picked up.

"A lot of my fellow swimmers and our support paddlers were also going off course ... I was swimming as hard as I could [and] I realized I wasn't moving," she said.

"It was a scary moment."

Tiana Langedyk says she was among the participants to be blown off course as winds picked up and currents swelled. (Marc D'Amours/CBC)

Karlyn Pipes, a former lifeguard and past participant in Across the Lakes, watched the event from shore and said she could see dozens of participants and paddlers being taken off course as they came to the middle of the water.

"On either side it was relatively calm, but as soon as they hit the middle ... they were getting pushed out into the water," she said.

Even the fastest swimmers, she said, were being challenged.

Safety measures

Pipes said it would have been difficult for organizers to anticipate the challenges.

The wind seemed to pick up mid-race, she said, and once people started being pushed around there was no choice but to continue.

Karlyn Pipes, a former lifeguard and past participant in Across the Lake, said there were lots of flotation devices and safety paddlers providing support to swimmers. (Chris Hromek)

"You can't sit there and say everybody get in a boat. If you look at the video, there were hundreds of water safety [craft] out there," she said, adding that there were many instances of people being helped as they encountered problems.

Pipes suggested future events could mandate the inclusion of flotation devices tied to participants so they have something to cling onto if they encounter problems.

"I have swum in races in Europe and it is mandatory of adults," she said.

Investigation ongoing

Pipes said it would be useful to know if the individual who died had a flotation device, and she also had questions about whether he may have encountered a medical emergency that led to him being unconscious out on the water.

"If he had a medical condition or something, this is different than somebody who just got overly tired and couldn't continue," she said, offering her condolences to family.

RCMP have called the death a drowning, but have referred the case to the B.C. Coroners Service for an official cause of death.

The coroner's office says it doesn't usually provide details due to privacy concerns and it may be several months before its investigation is completed.

It marks the fifth death on Okanagan Lake in the past few weeks.

World.title: Friends, family mourn 22-year-old killed in wrong-way crash with Sask. Roughrider
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Friends and family are mourning Bhishma Rajyaguru, who ​​d​ied​ Saturday evening ​after ​Saskatchewan Roughrider​ Jayden Dalke crashed into his vehicle.

The CFL player was driving the wrong way on a divided highway, with cannabis and alcohol in his SUV, according to RCMP.

Both Dalke and Rajyaguru were pronounced dead at the scene.

Friend Dakshesh Raval said Rajyaguru, 22, was driving back to Regina from Saskatoon when the crash happened on Highway 11 near Lumsden, Sask.

Raval said he knew something was wrong when Rajyaguru didn't pick up his phone calls.

"If you're calling him, he will not even let the phone ring twice," he said, adding Rajyaguru was often the first person he would call in a crisis.

"I started calling him, and he didn't pick it up once, twice. And on the third phone, I was already crying," Raval said.

Rajyaguru was a 'fantastic percussionist' and played the octapad in Regina Music Group, his friend and bandmate Dakshesh Raval says. (Vashisth Trevedi/CBC)

"I was like, please, God, please. It shouldn't be true."

Raval met Rajyaguru through a community cricket game almost four years ago.

Rajyaguru came to Regina from India as a student in April 2022, he said.

After discovering their shared love of folk music from the Indian state of Gujarat, Raval said the two formed the Regina Music Group along with four other musicians.

"He was doing it not for money. It was just his passion, his interest in music," he said.

"He was a fantastic percussionist, and he played the octapad."

Raval said he'll miss playing music with Rajyaguru, who he said was more like a brother to him.

"My stage will be empty forever on that side," he said.

"I cannot describe in words what I've lost, what his family has lost and what his parents are feeling."

WATCH | CFL player Jayden Dalke was driving wrong way on highway before crash: Roughriders’ Jayden Dalke drove wrong way on highway before crash: RCMP | Duration 2:02 Saskatchewan RCMP say Roughriders player and captain Jayden Dalke was driving the wrong way down a highway when he crashed into another SUV. Both drivers died. Police also said Dalke's vehicle was tied to a reported gas-and-dash half an hour earlier.

Raval said Rajyaguru had been looking forward to playing at Garba in the Park, an event put on by the Gujarati Samaj of Saskatchewan to celebrate folk dance and music.

The event, which was scheduled for July 25, has been postponed out of respect for Rajyaguru and his friends and family.

Raval and Viraj Mistry, another member of Regina Music Group, started a GoFundMe to help raise money to send Rajyaguru's remains to his parents in India. As Monday, the fundraiser reached over $77,000, surpassing its goal of $50,000.

Mistry said he remembers Rajyaguru's passion and dedication to his family.

"We all have aspirations, and we all have that one motive that we become successful and make it big in another country and build our own empire," he said.

"Bhishma had that same aspiration, and he had that same spark in his eyes to make it big, to do well and to prove to his family and everyone that loves him that he can achieve and make it big."

With their efforts focused on getting Rajyaguru's remains home, Mistry said the other band members haven't had much time to grieve.

"We are so busy making Bishma reach to his family. And obviously, there are ups and downs right now," he said.

"We cry at the moment. We laugh. We have so many memories."

World.title: India's 'cockroach' protesters vow to remain in New Delhi after police use tear gas, batons
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Supporters of India's youth-led Cockroach movement said Tuesday they will continue their protest in New Delhi, refusing to leave their sit-in site a day after police used tear gas and batons to disperse thousands of them as they tried to march toward parliament.

Hundreds of protesters remained camped at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site, under heavy police presence, saying they would stay until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns over alleged failures in India's examination system.

WATCH | The origins of the Cockroach movement: India’s Cockroach Party: Frustrated Gen Zs prove hard to crush | Duration 4:39 An online satirical jab at India’s government has exploded into a political movement on the streets. For The National, CBC’s Susan Ormiston breaks down the origins of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and how Gen Z frustrations are fuelling its rise.

"We are going to continue our protest," said Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

Monday's confrontation between protesters and police has become one of the most significant moments in the CJP's two-month campaign, which began as a satirical protest but quickly evolved into a nationwide, youth-led movement focused on exam leaks, unemployment and government accountability.

Activists and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party clash with police during a protest demanding the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged exam irregularities in New Delhi on Monday. (Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images)

Video of police beating protesters with batons and dragging demonstrators away spread quickly on social media, fuelling public outrage.

A security force personnel wields his baton in New Delhi Monday. (Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters)

Some footage showed young protesters crying and pleading with officers not to hit them, while others captured a defiant scene of youths standing their ground and enduring baton strikes.

Delhi Police said nearly 180 people were injured, including 118 security personnel and 60 protesters.

Police detain a CJP supporter in New Delhi on Monday. (Manish Swarup/The Associated Press)

Sona Bisht, a 20-year-old student who was part of the protest, said the confrontation with police had strengthened her resolve.

"If the government thinks that doing this with Gen Z, they can stop us, then that won't happen. We are here talking about education, talking about securing our future," she said.

After nearly a month of silence, the government made its first apparent move to engage with the protesters Monday, when a senior minister held talks with movement representatives. The outreach failed to ease tensions, with leaders saying they wanted action rather than assurances, including Pradhan's resignation, examination reforms and compensation for families of students who died by suicide after alleged exam irregularities.

Dipke accused authorities of breaking their word, saying police resorted to a baton charge after protesters were invited for talks.

Police use batons to disperse the crowd in New Delhi on Monday. (Manish Swarup/The Associated Press)

Rights group Amnesty International said in a statement late Monday that the police action showed "how peaceful dissent is being suppressed in India."

"The role of the authorities is to protect and facilitate peaceful protests, not to suppress them. The right to freedom of peaceful assembly is recognized under international human rights law and the Indian constitution," it said.

The movement, drawing students, professionals and families, marks a rare public challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in its third term, reviving criticism over its handling of dissent and its use of force to respond to protests. It gained momentum over the weekend after prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose three-week hunger strike has become a symbol of the protests, was forcibly taken to a hospital by police.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk undertakes an indefinite hunger strike with Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, in the foreground, in New Delhi on July 14. (Manish Swarup/The Associated Press)

Rabina Kashyap, a 26-year-old working professional, said she joined the protest on Tuesday after seeing police use tear gas and baton charges against students.

"I have nothing to do with this protest," she said. "But this is India, this is my country, and these are my people. So I will stand by them."
