We are taking a brief pause from our coverage of the Cockroach Janta Party protests to give you a roundup of other major developments in India today.

Sikkim tunnel blast leaves 10 dead, several missing

At least 10 people have died in India's Himalayan state of Sikkim after a suspected gas explosion triggered a tunnel collapse.

The incident occurred on Monday at state-owned National Hydroelectric Power Corporation's (NHPC) project on the Teesta river in Samardung village.

Seventeen others are feared trapped, local police chief Sonam Dolma told the media.

The NHPC said that a sudden burst of gas, ‌suspected to be methane trapped or embedded in rocks ​in the tunnel, caused an explosion, dispersing fumes and toxic gas.

Rescuers are struggling to get to those trapped due to the hazardous gases inside the tunnel.

India summons Russian diplomat after Indian seafarers killed in Ukraine ship attack

India on Tuesday summoned a senior Russian diplomat in New Delhi to protest an attack on a cargo ship leaving Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa that killed four Indian nationals.

India's foreign ministry said it conveyed "grave concerns and unequivocal condemnation of the attack" to the Russian Chargé d'Affaires Vladimir Ladanov.

Commercial vessel MV Golden Leo was attacked on Sunday. It had five Indian nationals on board.

The ministry said in a statement that it had urged Ladanov to convey to Moscow "India's strong concerns" that "the targeting of commercial shipping and the resulting loss of innocent civilian lives are unacceptable and must be avoided".

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Moscow was in touch with New Delhi on the issue.

"We are explaining our ⁠position. ​Most importantly, our armed forces are striking - ​and will continue to strike - vessels involved in transporting ammunition, weapons, ​and so on for ‌the purposes of the Kyiv regime," Peskov said.

World.title: 'Antifa' song climbs to top of charts after TV show cancellation
World.content:
German rapper Danger Dan and pianist Igor Levitt had been invited to play a song for the 100th episode of a political satire show on TV. The performance was canceled at the last minute due to its message.

German singer-songwriter Danger Dan and pianist Igor Levit were invited to perform a song titled "Keine Angst” (No Fear) for the 100th episode of a political satire TV show called "Die Anstalt" (The Institution). But shortly before the recording of the program, public broadcaster ZDF withdrew the invitation.

The sudden cancellation is sparking discussions on freedom of artistic expression and the limits of political speech in Germany. It is also drawing attention to the new song, which reached the top of the country's YouTube music charts shortly after the musicians decried the cancellation on June 17.

The broadcaster argued that parts of the lyrics could be interpreted as endorsing political extremism, vigilantism or violence against far-right activists, noting that this would conflict with ZDF's programming guidelines.

Show hosts condemn cancellation

"Die Anstalt" combines in-depth, single-topic investigations and political comedy. In the special 100th episode, titled "Die ANTIFAnstalt," the comedians analyzed the program of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is currently the most popular political party in Germany, all while civil rights groups are assessing it for potential unconstitutionality and ban proceedings.

The episode airs on television on Tuesday evening and is already available online .

The cancellation was not left uncommented during the show.

Instead of the song, an empty stage with a piano and microphones was shown during the program. After a few seconds of dead air, the hosts discussed the controversy, noting that the lyrics had been submitted to the broadcasting directors weeks ahead of the recording and that their plan was to openly discuss the lyrics with the author after the performance.

"We understand that opinions on the song may be divided, but we simply consider ZDF's decision to be spineless — especially at a time when right-wing extremist violence has once again reached a record high in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany," said one of the show hosts, Claus von Wagner.

The team took turns reading out and commenting on passages from the song, pointing out the sections that could be interpreted as criminal offenses or calls to violence.

What the song is about

The song offers a step-by-step guide on how to organize local, leaderless structures aimed at countering far-right movements. It advocates strict operational security, such as avoiding digital footprints and relying on face-to-face communication. It also describes tactics for investigating political opponents and publicizing their identities and affiliations, a practice often referred to as "outing" or doxing.

The lyrics also include references to militant action and express solidarity with individuals who have been found guilty of leading violent attacks on neo-Nazis.

ZDF director Norbert Himmler said he stood by the decision to cancel the performance: "In my view, the lyrics unquestionably provide instructions for a leftist resistance willing to use violence," he told the German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung.

At the same time, he admitted that his station should have handled the case differently: "We can be faulted for the last-minute cancellation," he said, adding, "We should have asked ourselves basic questions earlier — ideally before inviting the artists."

Eight members of the ZDF Television Council have criticized the broadcaster over the cancellation. In an open letter published on Monday by the online outlet netzpolitik.org, the council members argued that ZDF missed an opportunity to spark a debate about right-wing extremism in Germany and the various ways to combat it.

Danger Dan: Testing the limits of freedom of art

Danger Dan, whose real name is Daniel Pongratz, is known for his politically charged lyrics.

He is active as a member of the hip-hop band Antilopen Gang and as a solo artist. Lyrics on his debut solo album from 2008 already dealt with antisemitism in German rap.

Igor Levit and Danger Dan performed together for ZDF in 2021 Image: Rainer Keuenhof/picture alliance

His best-known hit came out in 2021. The single "Das ist alles von der Kunstfreiheit gedeckt" (That's All Covered by Freedom of Artistic Expression) deliberately tests the boundaries between protected artistic expression and potentially defamatory speech, and sharply criticizes right-wing politicians and public figures.

Igor Levit is a globally renowned pianist who is also widely recognized for his social activism, political engagement and public commentary. He had already accompanied Danger Dan on the piano in April 2021 for the live TV performance of the protest song "Das ist alles von der Kunstfreiheit gedeckt" on another program, "ZDF Magazin Royale."

Danger Dan and Igor Levit are now offering a substitute concert on Tuesday evening at Berlin's Columbia Theater. The show, "Die keine Angststalt" (a wordplay combining the title of the song with that of the TV show), will also be broadcast on YouTube.

According to reports, proceeds from ticket sales will go to the association Opferperspektive, described as "the central point of contact in Brandenburg [the state surrounding Berlin] for victims of right-wing, racist and antisemitic violence."

World.title: Germany: Mass shooting suspect found dead in prison
World.content:
A man suspected of carrying out one of the worst mass shootings in recent German history was found dead in his cell after an apparent suicide.

The Justice Ministry of Germany's state of Lower Saxony confirmed on Tuesday that the man suspected of killing six people at a youth and womens' shelter in the town of Stade last month had died by suicide.

Identified as Fatih Khan G. due to Germany's privacy laws, the ministry said there was "no indication of third-party involvement" in his death.

What happened in Stade?

G. is believed to have opened fire at the center for mothers and children, killing six welfare workers.

According to authorities, his three-month older daughter and her 34-year-old month were residing there. He had been in a custody dispute with his former partner over the baby, who showed signs of shaken baby syndrome.

He had reportedly previously threatened a doctor at a medical practice where his daughter had been seen.

He came to the shelter on June 29 to allegedly discuss accusations he had physically abused the baby. G. attempted to flee in a car but was caught shortly thereafter by police.

World.title: China narrows AI gap, challenges US influence
World.content:
At the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, Beijing showcased advances in AI while promoting its vision of open-source development and global governance.

As China narrows the artificial intelligence (AI) gap with the United States, Beijing is promoting a narrative centered on "open source" and "inclusive AI" as an argument for its vision of global governance.

During his keynote speech at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai on Friday, Chinese President Xi Jinping expressed China's ambition to take a leading role in setting global standards in AI. He criticized what he described as the "overextension of the concept of national security."

Xi did not openly reference the United States. However, Beijing's effort to position itself as an advocate of a new AI order and challenge US dominance was unmistakable.

This year's Shanghai summit sent several important signals, says Rogier Creemers, assistant professor at Leiden University in the Netherlands specializing in China's digital technology policy. The WAIC indicates that artificial intelligence is now one of Beijing's political priorities, and that China intends to compete with the United States by supporting open-source AI models and promoting AI-driven industrialization, Creemers told DW. He also noted China hopes to win support from countries in the Global South for this effort.

Beijing closing the AI gap

China is steadily narrowing the gap with the United States in AI model development, and its efforts at AI application in industrial processes are slowly maturing.

China's President Xi Jinping said artificial intelligence should not be dominated by a single country Image: Ng Han Guan/REUTERS

Chinese AI model developers have continued to keep pace on the global stage, largely by training open-weight models on limited but advanced computer hardware, Paul Triolo, senior vice president for China and tech policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, told DW.

Triolo believes deployment of AI across Chinese enterprises may be progressing faster than in the United States.

In addition, there is less fear of AI among the Chinese population than there is in the US, facilitating more rapid uptake of AI applications at the consumer level.

Earlier this year, Chinese state media claimed that the performance gap between Chinese and US AI models had "largely disappeared."

Several experts broadly agreed with this assessment, saying that certain benchmark tests of China's large language models (LLMs) such as GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 showed the gap narrowing or even fully closing.

For most applications, Triolo noted, China's leading open-weight AI models are cheaper to run and more than capable of handling most tasks.

At the same time, advanced proprietary models from leading US companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google still retain advantages in areas such as security and scalability.

Has the US 'AI firewall' worked?

In January 2025, the US Commerce Department expanded AI-related export controls through its "Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion," covering advanced computing chips, certain AI model weights and access to large-scale AI computing infrastructure.

The US also boosted export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment intended for China.

Laila Khawaja, research director at Gavekal Research, told DW that the US has been partially successful.

The controls have indeed impacted China's ability to manufacture chips domestically, cheaply, and at scale.

As for export controls on advanced AI chips, however, Khawaja notes that a significant amount of chips is still entering China through the gray market, while Chinese firms can still access computing resources through overseas cloud services.

According to Triolo, the evidence so far suggests the US strategy of slowing down China's advanced AI development has failed at many levels. At the same time, it caused massive collateral damage to US companies, especially to to their budgets for research and development and their supply chains, such as those delivering rare earths.

China's open-source AI push

In his keynote speech, Xi emphasized the importance of "encouraging open-source development."

Humanoid robots prepared meals inside the WAIC and directed traffic at intersections outside the exhibition halls Image: China News Service/VCG/IMAGO

Chinese state media have likewise promoted the message that China "does not pursue technological blockades."

Analysts say Beijing is increasingly framing "open source" and "inclusive AI" as its own narrative to counter the United States' largely closed-source AI ecosystem.

Chinese AI models are largely open-weight, with leading offerings such as DeepSeek, Zhipu's GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3 released under MIT licenses that allow users to download, deploy, modify, distribute and commercialize them.

Creemers noted that, for the time being, Chinese AI models are quite open in weight, but slightly less open in source.

According to Creemers, China hopes to encourage the rest of the world to adopt Chinese AI models, thereby creating overseas markets for Chinese technology and ensuring that China remains part of the next wave of technological development.

China's WAICO challenges Pax Silica

In Shanghai, Xi also announced that the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), an initiative launched by China, has already attracted 29 member countries.

He described the organization as "an important milestone in the history of AI development" and said it responds to calls from Global South countries for a greater role in AI governance.

Can Europe keep up with the US, China in the high-tech race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

WAICO is seen as an initiative to counter the US-led Pax Silica international initiative which aims to secure ​global AI and critical mineral supply chains.

The real competition, according to Triolo, lies in which parts of the US and Chinese AI technology stacks are ultimately adopted by countries in the Global South.

He believes China holds a significant advantage due to lower costs and the extensive digital infrastructure already built by Chinese companies such as Huawei across many developing countries.

Looking ahead

Overall, experts believe that the US will continue to lead in AI hardware design and compute capacity, while China could seize the lead on model innovation and will come to lead on AI diffusion.

Creemers argued that China's biggest structural disadvantage remains the lack of trust from countries in the Global North.

At the same time, US export controls continue to leave Chinese companies facing shortages of advanced AI computing hardware, limiting their ability to rapidly scale inference capacity to meet growing demand.

Looking ahead, Creemers argues that the rise of China's AI sector represents a broader historical shift.

"We need to understand that we are now facing, for the first time in modern history, a non-Western technological superpower," he said.

In his view, the future will not be defined by a singular global technological sphere, but rather by "a complex of overlapping technological networks and processes."

World.title: Is Germany investing in the right weapons?
World.content:
Germany wants to build up its army and pour hundreds of millions of euros into its defenses. But in a world where the battlefield is increasingly dominated by cheap drones, how many expensive tanks does the country need?

The German government's efforts to modernize and expand its military, the Bundeswehr, is in danger of being derailed by the country's slow procurement processes, according to critics.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran have shown that drones costing just tens of thousands can be an effective against weapons that devoured countless millions to develop and manufacture. Ukrainian air defenses, for example, have shown that they are able to hold their own against Russian attacks despite the fact that the Ukraine air force has only a fraction of the number of fighter jets and bombers.

Meanwhile, Germany has massively boosted its defense spending in the past few years. On top of the €100 billion ($114 billion) "special fund" announced following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the state has been rapidly raising its regular defense spending: From €62.4 billion in 2025 to €82.7 billion in 2026, with plans to raise that to €152 billion by 2029.

But critics are wondering whether these vast sums are being spent in the best way, not least since FCAS Franco-German fighter jet, which cost over €100 billion, was scrapped in June.

Respected defense analyst Nico Lange, who once worked for the German Defense Ministry, gave a scathing verdict on the current strategy. "It's the same dysfunctional system as before. They're just pouring significantly more money into it," he told the news portal Web.de. "The point is: Unless you actually change the structures of military planning and procurement, nothing better will come of it."

Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany learning its procurement lessons

Germany is currently climbing a steep learning curve, according to some politicians. Andreas Schwarz, Social Democrat member of the Bundestag defense committee, said the war in Ukraine is "completely changing how war is being fought."

On a visit to Ukraine earlier this month, Schwarz found that the debates that had dominated German politics in the first year of the war — about whether Germany should send Taurus rockets or Leopard tanks to help Ukraine — had become entirely irrelevant.

"When I was in Ukraine last week and visited the Defense Ministry, no one asked me about a Taurus cruise missile or a Leopard tank," he told DW. "What they need is help with drones, with ammunition, with modernizing their IT sector, with satellites and communication."

Can an army still fight with 'legacy' weapons?

But the Ukrainian experience doesn't mean that heavy weapons systems — often called "legacy systems" have become obsolete, as some analysts have been arguing in recent months. Max Becker, policy fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) , said that the Ukrainian war had shown, on the contrary, that tanks or artillery systems were still important to capture and hold territory, as well as for long-range strikes.

"It's about having the right mix of legacy systems, which you still need, and drone technology," he told DW. "That is a dilemma, because on the one hand you still need to invest in very expensive systems like combat tanks, which take a long time from order to delivery, but you also have to invest in systems like drones and loitering munitions."

The Ukrainian military, Becker added, had only developed its drone-based strategy partly out of necessity, because of its lack of conventional artillery and combat tanks. "I think the scenarios that Germany and NATO are preparing for are very different from those of the war between Russia and Ukraine, because NATO has very different equipment."

Andreas Schwarz also thinks that the Bundeswehr still needs the old weapons. "I don't want to say that we don't need tanks anymore — not at all, we're always going to need them," he said. "But the question is: Do we still need them in that quantity? And could I not complement or even optimize them with smaller, more flexible units?"

Drones are not only becoming more sophisticated, but also easier and cheaper to control — whereas expensive special computer systems were vital in the past, some military drones can now be steered with apps on a smartphone. Schwarz believes that though the German government and defense industry has grasped this new reality, but it still needs some time to implement the necessary measures to deal with it.

Why Germany struggles to recruit women soldiers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The procurement problem

The devil is in the detail — or, as so often, in the bureaucracy. Defense procurement is notoriously slow and complicated, and has proved especially so in a country where the arms industry is dominated by major companies like Rheinmetall that have made a lot of money building tanks and submarines for the world's militaries.

"We have an arms industry that for decades has relied on certain tried-and-tested technologies," said Schwarz. "Of course, we also have an army that has spent decades preparing for scenarios that are no longer very likely today. And of course, it’s difficult to establish this new way of thinking when we’ve been operating on the basis of different scenarios up until now — which requires those in charge to be willing to rethink their approach."

In an attempt to speed things up, the German government introduced a new law at the beginning of the year, whose name is as self-explanatory as it is unwieldy: the Bundeswehrbeschaffungsbeschleunigungsgesetz — or, the Military Procurement Acceleration Law.

This measure hopes to decentralize procurement by raising price thresholds so that certain purchases can be made without extra decision-makers being looped in, and removing paperwork for defense procurements between governments.

These are all good things, said Becker, because they help to change the received logic of defense procurement: In a world where drones and weapons can become obsolete within weeks, it makes no sense to make an order and then stockpile weapons that will be outdated in months.

"You create this new logic by agreeing innovation clauses in the procurement process, which obligate the companies to update their systems," Becker said. Seeing that the German government had grasped that such innovations were important had given him hope, he said.

What Germany should be concentrating on, he said, was setting up a new manufacturing infrastructure that can react quickly to new orders. "I can't buy a million drones," he said. "I need a stockpile of drones for training, and for exercise purposes, but I also need the industrial capacities so that the production of a mass of drones can be set up within four to six weeks."

The German military is also in the middle of a massive recruitment drive that is proving unpopular among young people — but, despite the increased automation of warfare, Schwarz believes that new human recruits are still essential. "We still need those people as drone pilots for example, but we also need people who can work with this technology," he said. Not only that, he added, new recruits were necessary to strengthen the reserve army to protect German territory for the worse case scenario.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

World.title: El empresario Julio Martínez se ratifica ante el juez al señalar a Zapatero por el rescate de Plus Ultra, pero afirma que no sabe con quién habló
World.content:
El empresario Julio Martínez Martínez ha ratificado este martes ante el juez José Luis Calama, instructor del caso Plus Ultra en la Audiencia Nacional, el escrito que envió el lunes al magistrado para señalar a José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero como la persona que “marcaba los pasos a seguir” en las gestiones que desembocaron en el rescate de 53 millones de euros que la compañía aérea recibió del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez tras la pandemia de coronavirus. Varias fuentes presentes en el interrogatorio inciden en que el imputado, que ha declarado durante cerca de tres horas tras imprimir un giro de guion a su estrategia y ofrecerse a “colaborar” con la justicia, ha implicado al expresidente en los trabajos para la aerolínea, pero ha sostenido que no sabe si el antiguo jefe del Ejecutivo intermedió ante alguien para agilizar la ayuda.

Como ya avanzó en el escrito enviado a la Audiencia Nacional, Martínez Martínez solo ha contestado este martes a las preguntas del magistrado (que lo ha interrogado durante alrededor de una hora y cuarto), de la Fiscalía Anticorrupción y de su propia defensa. El administrador de la consultora Análisis Relevante no ha querido responder a las acusaciones populares, encabezadas en este sumario por el PP. La cita ha comenzado con las cuestiones del juez Calama. Y después ha llegado el turno del ministerio público, representado por la fiscal Elena Lorente.

Fuentes jurídicas señalan que Martínez ha contado al juez que él empezó trabajando para Plus Ultra ante la administración de Venezuela y que, más tarde y tras la pandemia, extendió su labor a España. Según estas fuentes, el empresario ha recalcado incluso que aterrizó en el país sudamericano gracias al exlíder socialista, donde llegó a tener como interlocutora a la entonces vicepresidenta del Estado chavista, Delcy Rodríguez. A ella también la conoció a través del propio Zapatero, según ha apostillado.

El empresario ha venido a perfilar al expresidente como una persona que canalizaba sus contactos a través de Análisis Relevante y otras sociedades, mientras que él era solo un mero transmisor de las directrices que iba marcando el exdirigente socialista. En esta línea, según las fuentes consultadas, el juez ha llegado a calificar a Martínez Martínez como una especie de “correveidile”.

El empresario ha contado que Análisis Relevante cobraba por los informes y las gestiones de Zapatero, y luego él pagaba al expresidente. Como ya expuso en el escrito entregado el lunes, Martínez Martínez ha explicado que cuando el rescate de Plus Ultra empezó a ser cuestionado, la consultora y la aerolínea acordaron diferir el pago a lo largo del tiempo y que parte de esas cantidades se facturaran a otras sociedades del empresario. “En total, la cuantía abonada en concepto de honorarios por mediar en la obtención de la ayuda pública ascendió, aproximadamente, al 1% de la cantidad obtenida conforme a lo acordado”, especificaba el documento remitido al instructor José Luis Calama.

El empresario Julio Martínez, a su llegada a la Audiencia Nacional este martes junto a su abogada María Dolores Márquez de Prado. Claudio Álvarez

En el escrito entregado en la Audiencia Nacional, Martínez Martínez expuso que Análisis Relevante y Plus Ultra firmaron en julio de 2020 un contrato de 5.000 euros al mes “en concepto del asesoramiento que desde mayo venía dando” Zapatero. A ese contrato se le sumó otro, directamente vinculado a la obtención del rescate, que estipulaba el pago por parte de una aerolínea de una comisión del 1% de la financiación obtenida (unos 530.000 euros) en concepto de “contraprestación a los servicios prestados y al éxito de la operación” ante la SEPI. La Policía Nacional intervino una copia de este documento en el registro del domicilio de Martínez Martínez.

Julio Martínez Martínez ha entrado en la Audiencia Nacional sobre las 08.45 de este martes, acompañado de su abogada María Dolores Márquez de Prado. El empresario ha llegado al tribunal dispuesto a ratificar el escrito enviado un día antes al juez José Luis Calama, donde apuntaba directamente contra el expresidente y mostraba su disposición a “colaborar y contribuir al esclarecimiento de los hechos”. “En su faceta de consultor, era Rodríguez Zapatero quien marcaba los pasos a seguir”, incide el documento firmado por el dueño de Análisis Relevante.

“Zapatero quedó fuera del accionariado [de Análisis Relevante] y órganos formales de la empresa, pero era quien la lideraba y decidía todas aquellas cuestiones de estrategia y captación de clientes”, ahondaba el escrito de Julio Martínez Martínez, que también implicaba al exlíder socialista por el rescate de la aerolínea. Una maniobra que inflige un enorme daño a la defensa del exlíder del PSOE, que se desvinculó ante el juez de las ayudas a Plus Ultra. De hecho, en las últimas horas, el exjefe del Ejecutivo ha recibido más severos golpes, propinados por dos directivos de la compañía aérea. El presidente Julio Martínez Sola y el director financiero. Ambos le han atribuido gestiones para favorecerles en la obtención de los 53 millones de euros de dinero público obtenidos durante la pandemia.

Referencias a las hijas

Durante la declaración, según explican fuentes jurídicas, el dueño de Análisis Relevante ha eludido algunas cuestiones y ha respondido con varios “no lo recuerdo” y “no lo sé” —por ejemplo, no ha profundizado en el origen del dinero en efectivo (286.000 euros) que encontraron en su casa—. Aun así, ha mantenido la línea marcada por su escrito y ha repetido que Zapatero le comunicó finalmente el 26 de febrero de 2021 que la SEPI iba a conceder el rescate a Plus Ultra. También ha asegurado que las hijas del presidente hacían labores de maquetación de informes y que, en algún momento, les siguió pagando por ser familia del exjefe del Ejecutivo.

El juez ha preguntado también a Martínez Martínez por la creación de una sociedad offshore en Dubái, que los investigadores creen que se ideó para desviar el dinero de la supuesta comisión pagada a cambio del rescate de la aerolínea. Fuentes jurídicas señalan que el imputado ha matizado que esa empresa fue solo un proyecto y no se llegó a constituir. Sin embargo, el empresario sí ha confirmado que, como sostienen los investigadores, la posibilidad de constituir esa compañía se planeó en una comida. El sumario apunta que fue en un restaurante de Madrid, Portonovo, y que el almuerzo fue gestionado por la secretaria de Zapatero, Gertrudis Alcázar, quien envió al establecimiento a un escolta del expresidente para hacer la reserva. Durante su declaración ante el juez el pasado 17 de junio, el exdirigente socialista afirmó no recordar si él estuvo en la comida donde se habló de ello y se desvinculó por completo del proyecto de creación. “Jamás en mi vida he oído hablar de una sociedad offshore”, se escudó Zapatero.

World.title: Una perspectiva insólita para pasar revista a medio siglo
World.content:
Miguel Prieto y Reyes Lluch son, desde hace 50 años, lectores de EL PAÍS. El abogado y la promotora cultural, ciegos y trabajadores de la ONCE, muestran en esta entrevista un ángulo diferente sobre cómo ha cambiado España y cómo lo ha contado este diario

Durante muchos años, Miguel Prieto (Sama de Langreo, Asturias, 1961) y Reyes Lluch (Tortosa, Tarragona, 1957) leyeron EL PAÍS con los ojos de otros. Amigos, compañeros o familiares les prestaban la voz para recorrer juntos unas páginas que terminarían formando parte de su educación sentimental. Hoy ambos son lectores autónomos, la revolución digital ha traído eso: accesibilidad. Entre una escena y otra han transcurrido cinco décadas de historia de España; la evolución de un país que, también él, gracias a la labor de instituciones como la ONCE, aprendió a mirar de otra manera a las personas con discapacidad.

Prieto, abogado, procede de la cuenca minera asturiana, se crio en ese ambiente metalúrgico de obreros con afilada conciencia social, aunque la suya, cuenta, no vivió el despertar hasta que ingresó en la facultad. Al poco de nacer comenzaron sus severas dificultades de visión, obstáculo que no frenó un día a día agitado, donde las pasiones del niño y luego del joven se disfrutaban con absoluta intensidad. Como el ciclismo. Dicen de él que fue un buen fondista, y lo cierto es que los aficionados a la bicicleta le deben un hito fundamental: gracias a Prieto, la Vuelta Ciclista a España incluyó en su recorrido la subida al Angliru. A sus manos llegó el reportaje de una revista de principios de los noventa: ‘Atrévete con el puerto más duro de España’. Prieto, por supuesto, quiso subir a testarlo, altímetro digital y lupa al cuello, para alcanzar a leer el registro de datos. Tras su experiencia, en 1997 envió una carta que llegó al patrón de la Vuelta: tenemos el Mortirolo español —en referencia a ese puerto alpino que supone una de las etapas cumbre del Giro. En 1999, el Angliru hizo su debut en la gran ronda española, y el resto es historia.

Habla

Miguel Prieto Licenciado en Derecho Aficionado al ciclismo: gracias a él, se incluyó la subida al Angliru en la Vuelta Ciclista”

EL PAÍS fue la voz de los jóvenes que en la Transición adquirieron conciencia política. Un diario con pensamiento, hondura y plumas imbatibles. Miguel Prieto. Licenciado en Derecho

La tarraconense Reyes Lluch encontró desde niña en la música la forma de expandir esas fronteras que las dificultades visuales parecían querer imponerle a su mundo. Estudió guitarra, y también piano y canto. Participó activamente en aquella vida cultural catalana que, en los años de la Transición, suponía el mejor síntoma para creer en un resurgimiento cierto. Y convirtió después eso que había nacido como vocación en profesión. En mucho más, en realidad, dado que Lluch consagró su carrera a promover que las artes sirvieran como herramienta de participación: gracias a ella, unos 1.600 actores y actrices ciegos o con discapacidad visual se han subido a las tablas de un teatro. Su palmarés es largo, aunque en él brilla con fulgor especial un premio Max.

Pregunta. ¿Dónde estaban el 4 de mayo de 1976, cuando salió el primer número de EL PAÍS? ¿Cuál fue su primer contacto con el diario?

Prieto. En ese momento vivía en Asturias, en Sama de Langreo, en los valles mineros, y estaba cursando primero del Bachillerato Unificado Polivalente, el BUP. Lo empecé justamente en septiembre del 75, y ese noviembre murió Franco, así que fíjate qué curso más movidito. Pero en mayo de 1976 yo era estudiante, no muy preocupado o interesado en la actualidad, tan solo en el deporte. Sí recuerdo, sin embargo, que había ejemplares de EL PAÍS en sitios para mí emblemáticos. Porque en el Langreo en el que crecí (me fui con 22 o 23 años) la conciencia social era muy avanzada. El obrero o el metalúrgico que trabajaba duramente en sus turnos de mañana, tarde o noche luego se iba a leer periódicos y libros a lo que se llamaba entonces el hogar del productor, lo que luego serían las casas del pueblo. No era un mero local sindical, era una construcción con bibliotecas, cines, la gente jugaba al dominó o las cartas. Y, bueno, pensemos lo que significaron en la España de aquella época de transformación política. El diario EL PAÍS comenzaba a ser moneda de curso común, la gente lo llevaba bajo el brazo; a medida que pasaban los años se consolidaba como una voz diferente a las hegemónicas de la época. Prendía en los jóvenes, en esos que adquirían conciencia política, como fue mi caso, en la universidad.

Lluch. En mayo del 76 yo era una niña de 17 años que vivía en Tortosa (Tarragona) y todo mi grupo de amigas estaba preparándose para tener un futuro. Ese era nuestro interés. Queríamos un país más abierto, poder hablar de muchos temas. La publicación de EL PAÍS fue un soplo de aire nuevo, de libertad. Mis amigas lo leían y charlábamos, era una gran forma de análisis y debate. A mí me encantaba la sección de Cultura, porque yo era estudiante de música clásica, estudiaba guitarra y me encantaba leer las críticas de Enrique Franco. Cuando teníamos oportunidad, íbamos a escuchar conciertos: clásica, jazz, cantautores. EL PAÍS se ocupaba de hablar de los géneros emergentes. También prestaba atención a la literatura que nos interesaba, siempre nos fiábamos de sus recomendaciones sobre nuevos títulos publicados, libros interesantes, de sus críticas, leer su sección de Internacional... A mí que me gustaba muchísimo viajar, te abría las miras: siempre fue muy interesante cómo la enfocó el periódico. En Cataluña hablábamos dos idiomas, castellano y catalán, y mi familia, gracias a esa perspectiva que ofrecía, siempre trató de inculcarnos el valor de aprender otras lenguas y comunicarnos con gente diversa: fue una ayuda para tener la mente más abierta.

Reyes Lluch Promotora cultural Experta en teatro, música y artes plásticas: ganadora de un premio Max

Las dificultades de acceso a los medios escritos de las personas ciegas empezaron a solventarse con la prensa digital Reyes Lluch. Promotora cultural

Aquellos primeros años consolidaron una relación que se mantendría durante décadas. Para Prieto, EL PAÍS representaba una forma rigurosa de acercarse a la actualidad, con un periodismo de profundidad que encontraba difícilmente en otros medios. Lluch, por su parte, fue ampliando sus intereses desde las páginas culturales hacia los artículos de opinión, convencida de que una democracia madura necesita confrontar ideas y no únicamente consumir titulares.

Con el tiempo también cambió la manera de leer. Para ambos, la llegada de la edición digital supuso una transformación radical: la apertura definitiva de una puerta hacia la autonomía que durante décadas había permanecido, como mucho, entreabierta. Prieto la vivió como una evolución natural del periódico hacia otro ecosistema informativo. Lluch, en cambio, la recuerda con hondura: ya no dependería de nadie para leer. Esta evolución tecnológica la resumen fuentes de la ONCE: “En cuanto aparecieron los diarios web, las personas ciegas pudieron hacerse con distintos dispositivos que leían en alto aquello que estaba escrito en la pantalla para que pudiera escucharse. Había incluso aparatos que traducían los artículos a braille. Hoy, hay periódicos como EL PAÍS que, directamente, ofrecen la posibilidad de que una IA transforme en audio con una voz lineal y poco interpretativa —como prefieren las personas ciegas— cada uno de sus artículos”.

Si, como lectores de EL PAÍS, existe un día que ambos recuerdan con precisión fotográfica, es el 23 de febrero de 1981.

Pregunta. El 23-F es un día importante en la historia del diario, que lanzó una edición especial esa misma noche. ¿Qué estaban haciendo ese día y cómo recuerdan la actuación de los medios de comunicación?

Prieto. Eso lo tengo grabado en la memoria. Era lunes, yo estaba estudiando segundo de Derecho. Tenía que preparar un examen de derecho civil, justo ese año que se aprobó la ley del Divorcio. Yo entonces era una persona muy implicada. Cuando se publicó EL PAÍS reivindicando el estatus democrático de aquella España que daba un pasito para adelante y otro para atrás, con balbuceos, con atentados de ETA, el Grapo, la Triple A, atentados fascistas… significó muchísimo. La apertura vino enredada en mucha confusión. El martes 24 de febrero la mitad de mi clase quería entrar y seguir con las asignaturas como si nada; y la otra mitad señalaba el momento crucial de la historia que vivíamos. El gesto de EL PAÍS nos enseñó qué tipo de prensa necesitaba un proyecto de progreso con el que nos sentíamos representados.

En la imagen, la música y promotora teatral Reyes Lluch toca la guitarra.

Lluch. El 23-F me pilló volviendo del Conservatorio de Tarragona a Tortosa. Mi hermana, que vivía en Tarragona, me había acompañado al tren; yo subí al vagón y, como el resto de los que estaban ahí sentados, no me enteré de nada. Fue cuando por fin llegué a casa cuando fui consciente del tremendo golpe de Estado. Mis padres estaban en Valencia, tuvieron prácticamente los tanques en la puerta: fueron horas de mucha incertidumbre, de miedo, pendientes de la radio y la televisión. Hasta que salió el Rey. La edición especial de EL PAÍS, defendiendo la democracia y las libertades, el pacto constitucional, nos dio tranquilidad, nos ofreció la certeza de que nuestro país iba a continuar por la senda de la democracia.

Tanto Prieto como Lluch llegaron muy jóvenes a la ONCE y han permanecido en la organización una vida entera. Prieto se mudó a Madrid con 23 años y, desde el principio, mostró interés por participar en el asociacionismo que prestaba ayuda a las personas con discapacidad. Fue director adjunto del área de Juego de la ONCE y, actualmente, gestiona la unidad de Juego Responsable. Lluch, armada sempiternamente con una guitarra que no ha dejado de tocar, fue durante años responsable de Promoción Cultural de la ONCE: ha impulsado más de 40 grupos de teatro, con más de 45 montajes anuales de media; y también ha prestado apoyo a cientos de iniciativas literarias, musicales y de artes plásticas.

El diario deportivo AS daba cuenta en este reportaje de la hazaña de Miguel Prieto como descubridor del Angliru.

Ambos, cuando se paran a analizar el presente de España y cómo lo afronta la prensa, coinciden en el complejo desafío al que se enfrenta el periodismo de hoy, ese que, dice Prieto, de pronto da igual cabida a influencers que a buenos columnistas. Prieto echa de menos la profundidad intelectual, aquella sensación de que cada artículo ayudaba a comprender la realidad y no solo a reaccionar ante ella. Para Lluch, el mal mayor es la radicalización ideológica, la composición de informaciones donde, en su opinión, se percibe ya un sesgo intencional. La tarraconense lamenta la creciente polarización del debate público y reclama medios capaces de preservar la independencia y de favorecer una conversación democrática realmente fructífera, basada en el respeto a las opiniones diferentes.

Cinco décadas después, ambos se mantienen fieles al mismo periódico, a un diario EL PAÍS hoy global. Quizá por eso insisten tanto en el valor de la información con contexto, en la preservación del pensamiento crítico. Tras medio siglo, el objetivo no ha cambiado: están convencidos de que el periodismo todavía tiene la obligación de hacernos comprender mejor el mundo.

World.title: Lo que no puedes perderte si vas a Asturias de vacaciones este verano

Restaurantes, pueblos, playas, naturaleza y prerrománico en un destino ideal para ver el eclipse solar del próximo 12 de agosto

Sería injusto reducir los atractivos de Asturias a su clima fresco en verano. Pero es cierto que, en los últimos años, el imparable aumento de las temperaturas ha hecho que el Principado se haya convertido en la opción elegida por muchos para pasar las vacaciones. Asturias batió en 2025 su récord de turismo rural con 304.979 visitantes, según los datos que publicó el pasado mes de febrero el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Quienes elijan esta comunidad este verano, tienen muchas opciones para disfrutar de la naturaleza más allá de los Picos de Europa —aunque siempre merecen una visita— y para perderse por sus pueblos y aldeas. Además, Asturias también será un enclave estupendo para contemplar el eclipse total de sol del próximo 12 de agosto, ya que será total en toda la comunidad, como explica nuestra guía. World.title: Police seize servers of porn site Motherless in abuse inquiry
World.content:
Police have raided the hosting company of the pornography website Motherless at locations in Steenbergen, Rotterdam and Amsterdam, seizing servers used by the site, broadcaster NOS has reported.

The public prosecution department is investigating images of possible sexual abuse that appeared on the site, including images of child sexual abuse and of women being assaulted while drugged. Both the people who uploaded the material and the role of the site itself are under investigation, which will be carried out with Europol.

No one has been arrested so far.

Motherless, which had tens of millions of visitors a month, was taken offline by prosecutors in May after reporting by NOS and Nieuwsuur revealed large amounts of illegal material on its servers, hosted by Steenbergen-based provider Nforce. The site later reappeared online via other routes.

The raids are the latest step in a series of Dutch investigations connected to the site. In June, NOS revealed that moderators of the site had themselves posted images of child sexual abuse, with one employee alone uploading 110,000 images.

Earlier, an investigation by CNN had found some 20,000 videos on the site of women being filmed while drugged or asleep, and NRC reported that Dutch users were among those sharing such material.

World.title: Class ranking skews school advice for Dutch 12-year-olds: Study
World.content:
The school track advice Dutch children receive at the end of primary school is influenced by how they rank compared with their classmates, even when their test scores are identical, according to research by the Erasmus School of Economics.

Moving up around three places in the class ranking increases a pupil’s chance of a vwo recommendation, the highest track, by about 2.5 percentage points. On the other hand, children near the bottom of their class are more likely to be advised to go to vmbo (the lowest track), regardless of their actual ability.

The advice pupils are given at around age 12 largely determines which type of secondary school they can attend, and the study found that ranking children early on impacts their chances of going to university.

The research suggests teachers use rank as a shortcut because judging absolute ability is hard, while comparing classmates is easy.

The effect was stronger among more experienced teachers, and teachers proved more sensitive to the rankings of children from low-income families and ethnic minority backgrounds, who were more likely to be given lower advice than equally scoring children from better-off homes.

Earlier research has shown that girls and children outside the big cities also tend to receive lower advice than their scores warrant.

World.title: Frost in July: Twente records a midsummer first for Netherlands
World.content:
Parts of Twente woke to a touch of ground frost on Tuesday, something never before recorded in the Netherlands at the height of summer.

A temperature of -0.1° was briefly measured at 10 centimetres above the ground at around 5.30am, broadcaster NOS reported. According to weather bureau Weeronline, ground frost had never previously been recorded in the Netherlands between July 20 and August 21.

Since meteorologists began measuring ground temperatures in 1971, ground frost in July has occurred just nine times. The coldest reading, -1.6°, also came in Twente, on July 4, 2019 – a month that went on to produce the opposite extreme, with the hottest temperature ever measured in the Netherlands, 40.7° in Gilze-Rijen, following three weeks later.

Ground frost is slightly more common in June, and in 1955 frost was even recorded at the standard measuring height of 1.5 metres, when Witteveen in Drenthe registered -0.8°.

World.title: Dutch ban on Israeli settlement goods to start on September 22
World.content:
The Netherlands will ban the import of goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements from September 22, foreign minister Tom Berendsen has told MPs.

The cabinet announced the trade ban in May but had not yet set a date, broadcaster NOS reported. A majority of MPs called last year for a national ban on the import and transit of goods from illegal settlements in territories occupied by Israel.

The measure covers not only imports but also trading in settlement goods, and Dutch companies operating abroad will have to comply. Activities aimed at getting around the ban are prohibited as well. The measure will apply for three years in principle.

The Council of State raised no objections to the ban in an urgent advisory opinion, although it expressed doubts about how enforceable it will be, a concern the cabinet itself acknowledged when the measure was announced.

The government has repeatedly pushed for an EU-wide ban, but there is insufficient support among member states. Belgium, Spain and Ireland have already introduced sanctions at national level.

Last month, a report by legal organisation Global Echo found that the Netherlands is the top destination for Israeli settlement produce entering the EU market.

The building of settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights is a violation of international law, and according to the United Nations, settlers are systematically guilty of violence and intimidation against the Palestinian population.

“We want to prevent Dutch society, through its economic activities, from contributing to an unlawful occupation and the maintenance of illegal settlements,” prime minister Rob Jetten said when the ban was agreed in May.

World.title: Eindhoven students build world’s first solar-powered ambulance
World.content:
Students at Eindhoven University of Technology have unveiled what they say is the world’s first solar-powered ambulance, designed to bring medical care to remote regions where poor roads and a lack of fuel or electricity put healthcare out of reach.

Stella Juva, presented on Tuesday, was developed in a year by Solar Team Eindhoven, a group of 23 students. Solar panels on the roof power both the motor and the medical equipment on board, and on a sunny day the vehicle is expected to cover 715 kilometres without needing any charging infrastructure.

But how does a solar vehicle fare in one of Europe’s cloudiest countries? “The Dutch weather, to say the least, is not Kenya’s,” team manager Mathijs van Gerven told DutchNews after the launch. The ambulance’s 50 kWh battery stores solar energy so it can keep powering its equipment, and its own motors, without interruption, he explained.

Unlike a traditional ambulance, which transports patients to hospital, Stella Juva is designed to bring care to people, allowing healthcare providers to carry out blood tests, screen for diseases such as tuberculosis and malaria, administer vaccinations and perform pregnancy ultrasounds.

The students developed the vehicle with international health organisations including Amref Health Africa, formerly known as the Flying Doctors. “In remote areas, healthcare workers sometimes travel great distances by bicycle, and reliable energy is not a given,” Femke Maurits of Amref’s Dutch branch said in a statement.

Energy is essential, she said, for keeping vaccines cooled and running medical equipment.

Kenya test

In August the team will take Stella Juva to Kenya, starting with a kick-off at Amref International University attended by officials from the Dutch embassy and Kenyan diplomats. The vehicle will then be tested at two field locations, where healthcare scenarios, such as the treatment of tuberculosis patients, will be simulated.

“Three of our team members have been chosen to drive Stella Juva – they were the first to test her,” Van Gerven told us. “We will see who gets to drive the first Kenyan metres, but I reckon they will all want to go first.”

Afterwards, the ambulance will tour events across the Netherlands, and possibly Europe, to encourage companies and healthcare providers to take the concept further. For production at scale, the team is looking to industry.

“If 23 students are able to do this in just one year, think about what is possible if technological companies and social organisations collaborate,” Van Gerven said.

World.title: Lorries ignoring Merwedebrug ban face €500 fines
World.content:
Roads agency Rijkswaterstaat is installing traffic cameras on the damaged Merwedebrug near Gorinchem to enforce a ban on lorries, with fines of up to €500 for drivers who ignore it.

The bridge on the A27 has been closed since Saturday to freight traffic after an inspection found the bridge’s steel was weaker than expected in several places, and that it could no longer guarantee the structure would hold under heavy traffic.

The roads agency issued an urgent appeal to trucks to avoid using the bridge but many are still driving over it.

An NOS reporter on the scene counted dozens of trucks in half an hour, including vehicles with Dutch license plates.

The new ban will now be enforced via cameras which will automatically read the license plates. Enforcement will be done together with the police and the public prosecution service. Fines can be as high as €500.

Cars, vans, motorbikes, buses and emergency vehicles can still use the Merwedebrug. Freight traffic is being diverted via the A16 and the A2.

World.title: Deaths linked to online medicines prompt national study
World.content:
The addiction research institute Trimbos is starting an investigation into “self-medication”, people buying medicines online without consulting a doctor, it has told broadcaster NOS.

The study has been commissioned by health minister Sophie Hermans, who is worried about injuries and even deaths linked to medicines sold online.

Drugs bought online can be dangerous, according to Laura Smit-Rigter, national coordinator of drug monitoring and policy at Trimbos. “It could involve counterfeit medication,” she told NOS. “In that case, the dosage or composition of the product could be completely different. And that can be life-threatening.”

In 2025, two men who ran a webshop called Funcaps, which sold fake and illegal medicines to the general public, appeared in court in connection with the deaths of at least 27 people.

Funcaps sold a range of substances, among them bromazolam, a sedative, O-DSMT, an opioid painkiller, and 2F-ketamine, an anaesthetic. The products came with no package inserts or usage instructions, and sales were pushed with discount deals and sample packs.

Trimbos wants to find out how many people are buying medicines online and why they turn to the internet instead of going to their doctor.

World.title: Big firms hired 13,500 refugees and asylum seekers last year
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Large companies in the Netherlands hired 13,500 refugees and asylum seekers last year, in an effort to plug staff shortages in sectors such as logistics, hospitality and technical trades.

The figures come from Tent Nederland, a coalition of 51 major employers including Philips, IKEA, ABN Amro, Unilever, Arcadis and Randstad, and were reported by NU.nl. The jobs include both permanent positions and work via staffing agencies.

Tent Nederland was set up in April 2025 as the Dutch arm of the Tent Partnership for Refugees, a global network of large companies founded by Chobani boss Hamdi Ulukaya.

The organisation puts employers in direct contact with refugees, partly through regional job fairs organised with local councils and the refugee settlement agency COA.

Companies are finding it easier to reach refugees, director Hélène van Melle told NU.nl, including asylum seekers, who have been able to work year round since a court scrapped a 24-week annual limit at the end of 2023.

“Employers initially had great difficulty getting in contact with these people,” she said. “But within a year we are seeing that companies are open to taking on asylum seekers.”

Government target

Some firms are recruiting refugees by their own initiative. Construction group Heijmans, which is not a Tent Nederland member, has taken on 60 refugees with residence permits over the past two years.

The hirings fit with government plans to get 75,000 more refugees and promising asylum seekers into paid work by the end of 2030. Work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen wants 60% of new arrivals to have a proper job within five years of being given a residence permit.

Refugee employment has long lagged the rest of the workforce, although CBS figures published in May show new arrivals are finding work faster than a decade ago.

World.title: Poland joins EU satellite project developing European alternative to Starlink
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last week, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that it will open a new security centre in Warsaw. One of its areas of operation will be satellite communication, including the use of satellite imagery to monitor critical incidents such as natural disasters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also revealed that Poland and the ESA are working on the first Polish spacecraft, which would provide servicing, refuelling and other services for satellites Last year, Poland launched its first national military satellite. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
