(Photo source: the company)

World.title: Romania opens first large voluntary waste collection center in Cluj-Napoca
World.content:
Romania inaugurated its first large voluntary waste collection center in Cluj-Napoca, marking the start of a national network of 13 such facilities financed through the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). The new center is designed to help residents dispose of bulky and special waste that cannot be collected through regular household waste collection services.

The Environment Ministry said the project received more than RON 32.6 million in non-repayable European funding through the PNRR.

Covering 1.4 hectares, the facility includes dedicated collection platforms and containers, a chemical analysis laboratory, administrative buildings, a refrigerated storage room for animal carcasses, and a heavy-duty weighbridge to monitor waste flows.

The center accepts a wide range of waste, including bulky household items such as furniture and mattresses, construction and demolition waste, used tires, waste electrical and electronic equipment, textiles, wood waste, recyclable materials, biodegradable waste, and other waste streams that cannot be collected through the standard door-to-door system.

“This center addresses exactly the problems that have frustrated citizens for years. Where do we dispose of an old mattress, used tires, construction debris, furniture or a broken refrigerator? From today, the people of Cluj have a clear, modern and civilized solution," interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said.

She added that hundreds of smaller voluntary collection centers are expected to be completed across Romania in the coming months through the PNRR, saying the country is taking "a major step toward the European circular economy model, where waste becomes a resource.”

According to the ministry, the Cluj-Napoca facility is the first of 13 large voluntary collection centers planned nationwide. Similar projects are scheduled for cities including Craiova, Buzău, Brașov, Constanța, Iași, Bucharest, and Sibiu.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Facebook/Ministerul Mediului - România)

World.title: World-famous yogi Sadhguru to take the stage at Romania’s Untold festival
World.content:
Sadhguru, one of the world’s most renowned yoga masters and a New York Times bestselling author, will take the main stage of the Untold festival on August 6 to deliver a message about the importance of inner balance, well-being, and building a more conscious world before tens of thousands of people.

The famous yogi is known by hundreds of millions of people around the world for his programs dedicated to transformation and personal development through yoga and meditation, as well as for his global initiatives dedicated to the environment and society.

Sadhguru’s participation in the festival comes after a collaboration between Untold festival organizers and Conscious Music Circle (CMC), a collaboration between artists and music industry professionals whose lives have been deeply influenced by Sadhguru’s practices and teachings. The organization’s mission is to contribute to raising awareness through music, providing artists, industry professionals and communities with access to yoga and meditation tools developed by Sadhguru and promoting well-being in the music industry.

The partnership aims to promote mental health and awareness through scientifically validated yoga and meditation practices, integrated into festival and music culture, the organizers said.

Through this collaboration, Untold becomes the first major festival in the world to offer free access to the Miracle of Mind meditation app to all festival participants, artists and team members. The app will be integrated into the festival experience through special activations and dedicated sessions held throughout the four days of the festival.

“You cannot change the past. You can live the present. But you can build the future if you choose to do so. For the first time in history, we can be connected with all of humanity. If we want to transform the world, if we want to transform humanity, now is the time. Let’s do this together,” Sadhguru said in the press release.

The Untold festival will take place from August 6-9 in Cluj-Napoca, and this year’s edition brings more than 200 artists to the festival stages, including STING, Lewis Capaldi, Zara Larsson, Flo Rida, The Chainsmokers, Kygo, James Hype, Solomun, Carl Cox, Sara Landry, Holy Priest and many others.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: French group Syclef takes over Romanian industrial refrigeration player Horeco
World.content:
Syclef, which specializes in commercial refrigeration, industrial refrigeration, and HVAC (heating, ventilation, air conditioning), has taken over Horeco Holding, a Romanian group specializing in industrial refrigeration.

The transaction remains subject to obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals from the Romanian Competition Council and the Commission for the Examination of Foreign Direct Investments (CEISD).

Founded in 1995 and based in Buzău, in eastern Romania, Horeco Holding brings together two companies: Horeco Impex and Frigoclima. The group employs more than 90 people and reported revenue of over EUR 20 million.

Florin Niculescu, the current CEO, remains a shareholder and will continue to lead the company's management and strategic development.

The partnership with Horeco is the second transaction in Romania announced by Syclef this month. In early July, the group announced that Unicool, a Romanian group specializing in commercial refrigeration, was joining it.

Headquartered in Cluj county, Unicool was founded in 2011. The group gathers two companies: Unicool Instalatii Frig and Acsa Coolteam. The founders will remain shareholders in both companies and will continue to manage operations.

Syclef is present in France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, Ireland, Poland, Africa, the Indian Ocean region, and Romania. It designs, installs, and maintains custom technical solutions for a wide range of sectors.

World.title: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH

This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN.

“I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said.

Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions.

For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1.

If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price.

The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”.

It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff.

Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill.

Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum.

The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems.

Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious.

“This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei.

“It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country.

“It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added.

Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures.

The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism.

According to media reports, ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity.

Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases.

Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed.

The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored.

At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine.

Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview.

Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards.

“It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said.

“That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

World.title: Tests Show Faeces Contaminated North Macedonia Town’s Water Supply
World.content:
The centre of Gostivar, North Macedonia. Photo: Fazlijah/Wikimedia Commons.

Lab tests have confirmed the presence of faecal contamination in the drinking water supplied to the western North Macedonian town of Gostivar, local prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

The findings, disclosed by the Gostivar Basic Prosecutor’s Office, appear to prove that the town’s water supply is linked to an epidemic of gastrointestinal illness that has overwhelmed local health services since last week.

On Monday, police detained the head of the local public water utility, Artana Asani, and two other managers over the outbreak that has made more than 3,000 people sick so far.

The Gostivar Prosecutor’s Office said three officials are suspected of committing “serious crimes against the environment and nature through the pollution of drinking water.

“The suspects, acting together in their official capacities … made the drinking water in the overflow chamber of the system supplying Gostivar municipality and several surrounding villages unusable by introducing a harmful substance into it,” the Prosecution said.

The probe suspects the water supply became contaminated when the water company, in a presumed attempt to increase the water supply last month, connected additional pumps to the existing system that drew in water from an unhealthy surface-level source.

According to the prosecution, laboratory tests conducted by the Institute of Public Health detected faecal contamination in the water supply, including extremely high concentrations of coliform bacteria and the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli), indicating contamination with human or animal faecal matter and rendering the water unsafe to drink.

Before her arrest, water utility head Asani last week insisted the outbreak of illness in the town was not caused by water but food poisoning. But authorities pinpointed drinking water as the most likely culprit, given the sheer scale of the outbreak.

The outbreak has sent more than 3,000 people to hospitals and clinics with symptoms including severe stomach pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and nausea, making it one of the largest recorded waterborne health incidents in North Macedonia in decades.

The Health Ministry has warned that the flow of new patients is not subsiding yet and is running at about 200 to 300 new patients per day.

Meanwhile, tap water in the town of roughly 80,000 people, some 65 kilometres west of the capital, Skopje, is unusable, and the municipal and state authorities have sent trucks with bottled water for residents’ use.

The Health Ministry on Monday said some of the contaminants found in the system are not easy to deal with, so the ban on drinking tap water will likely stay in place for some time.

The incident has triggered widespread public anger, with residents questioning how contamination on this scale could have gone undetected until thousands of people had already become ill.

Gostivar Mayor Valbon Limani on Monday denied any responsibility for the crisis himself, saying he had no role in the water company.

“I do not feel any moral responsibility because the public utility company Komunalec is a separate legal entity that manages and operates the water supply system. Otherwise, the citizens who know me are aware that, had the situation been different, I would certainly have been the first to resign,” Limani said.

World.title: Hungarian PM’s Presidential Gambit Fails as Polgar Declines Nomination
World.content:
“The responsibility is entirely mine,” Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar admitted on Monday night, after he had failed to convince the world’s greatest female chess player of all time, Judit Polgar, to accept the nomination to be the country’s next president.

“I don’t feel the strength to take on the historic responsibility, therefore I am unable to accept the invitation,” Polgar, 49, posted last night, ending a day of intense speculation in Hungary and abroad.

Nominating a grandmaster as Hungary’s next president was just the latest in a series of unconventional moves by the government headed by Magyar’s Tisza party. It was a hasty decision by a government that seems to be under constant time pressure to deliver on the numerous promises it made during the campaign for the April 12 election, which it won by a landslide.

“The selection of Hungary’s next president should not be rushed, Peter Magyar is acting as if there were no time for a meaningful public debate about the country’s next head of state,” the human rights watchdog Amnesty International said in a statement.

Tamas Sulyok was regarded as an ideological presidential appointee of former prime minister Viktor Orban. According to Sulyok’s critics, he stood by as the previous government weakened democratic institutions and undermined the rule of law. As a result, voters had lost confidence in him, Magyar argued during the campaign, and his removal would be an essential step in rebuilding democracy and the system of checks of balances in Hungary.

Sulyok refused to budge for weeks until a constitutional amendment was passed on July 13 by the Tisza-dominated parliament which, among other measures, term-limited MPs to 12 years, pensioned off constitutional court judges at 70 and, in a single sentence, terminated the president’s mandate with immediate effect. Sulyok announced on Saturday he would sign the constitutional amendment, “fulfilling my obligation under the Fundamental Law [Hungary’s constitution] after carefully weighing my legal options and my conscience”.

In a lengthy video posted on Facebook, the outgoing president lamented the “end of constitutionalism” and warned that the Tisza government posed a threat to Hungarian democracy. The president has a largely ceremonial role but can block some legislation and delay appointments.

Hungary’s parliament now has 30 days to elect a new head of state, who will be in office until a new constitution is drawn up and adopted, but no longer than five years.

Magyar had promised broad public consultation in choosing the next president, saying he wanted a person capable of uniting Hungary’s deeply polarised society and representing the country abroad. But on Sunday, only hours after Sulyok had stepped down, a group of Hungarian intellectuals, athletes and public figures – mainly critics of the former Fidesz government but also some more aligned with it – published an open letter on Facebook endorsing Polgar for the presidency.

Magyar replied in a Facebook post that he would discuss the matter on Monday with Polgar, who he saw as the most suitable candidate. Tisza’s parliamentary group leader Andrea Bujdoso also described Polgar as the party’s preferred candidate for the presidency.

Some sensed a stitch-up after evidence emerged showing Magyar meeting with Polgar two weeks earlier at the US embassy’s Fourth of July reception in Budapest, where she quickly defeated the prime minister in a chess match. It remains unclear whether they discussed a possible political role before or after the event.

Polgar and her two older sisters were born into a Hungarian Jewish family and educated by their father, Laszlo Polgar, who developed an unconventional method aimed at proving that geniuses are made rather than born. The sisters did not attend school in Communist Hungary but instead spent eight to ten hours a day playing chess. The family travelled extensively around the world at a time when few Hungarians enjoyed such opportunities.

Polgar won her first championship at the age of nine and became the world’s highest-ranked female player at just 12. Throughout her career she played in the men’s league, and defeated several world champions, including Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov. “They thought I was this little girl with a cute ponytail, but I wasn’t that cute when I played,” she once said in an interview.

At the age of 15, she became the youngest grandmaster in history at the time, breaking Bobby Fischer’s longstanding record. A documentary of her life, Queen of Chess, was released earlier this year and became an instant hit on Netflix. Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has focused on educational initiatives and promoting chess among children. She is married to a veterinarian, has two children, and lives in Budapest.

Her potential nomination prompted a variety of reactions. Critics argued that Polgar has never shown any interest in politics and was never publicly critical of Orban’s government. Supporters argued it is an advantage that she has never been affiliated with any political party or movement, but is admired across the political spectrum as one of Hungary’s most accomplished and internationally respected public figures.

But most criticism was focused on the speed with which Tisza tried to rush through the nomination process, arguing that there had been little genuine public consultation despite the lack of urgency.

Fidesz politicians maintain that whoever is elected under the current circumstances will lack democratic legitimacy because of the manner in which the previous president was removed.

World.title: It’s Time NATO Stopped Ignoring Bosnia’s Ammunition Industry
World.content:
When NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned Allied defense ministers that Russia produces in three months what the entire Alliance produces in a year, Europe quickly moved.

Germany’s Rheinmetall accelerated artillery production across two countries. The US Army drove toward 100,000 155mm shells per month. Billions of euros poured into the EU’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production. Summits convened. A strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation was adopted. Commitments were signed.

What largely escaped notice in all those urgent conversations was a pair of factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only country currently in NATO’s Membership Action Plan.

Pretis d.d., located in Vogosca, near Sarajevo, and Binas d.d., in Bugojno, have operated quietly for decades, largely overlooked by NATO. Pretis is among the few facilities in Europe producing 155mm artillery shells to full NATO standards – the exact caliber at the center of the Alliance’s ammunition crisis.

World.title: ‘Obviously Dangerous’: Unlicensed Jet Skis Pose Growing Hazard on Albania’s Coast
World.content:
On September 11 last year, 18-year-old David’s holiday in Albania took an harrowing turn. The Czech teenager was riding a jet ski in Saranda Bay when there was an accident.

While returning to shore at low speed to pick up his mother, who was waiting to join him as a passenger, he was hit by another watercraft operated by tourists from France.

The impact left him unconscious in the water. His mother, who was filming from the pier, was shocked to see her son floating motionless on the surface, kept afloat only by his life jacket.

“My son fell into the water, remaining motionless and unconscious,” she told BIRN. David and his mother, who asked to remain anonymous, provided BIRN with the full case file, including footage showing the moment of the collision.

World.title: Serbia’s Media Regulator Resumes Work After EU Prompting
World.content:
Serbia’s new Council of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, held its first constitutive session on Monday but failed to elect a president. The Council is still not composed completely as its ninth member has not been elected yet.

The previous REM Council’s mandate expired in November 2024. Since then, Serbia’s parliament has failed to appoint a new Council. The selection process was marked by numerous allegations of irregularities. Establishing a fully operational REM Council was one of the European Union’s key demands for Serbia as part of its rule-of-law obligations in its EU accession process.

The establishment of the new Council was enabled after four members who had previously resigned agreed to assume their positions earlier in July.

Eight members of the new REM Council were elected in November 2025. However, the ruling majority in parliament did not vote for the ninth member, who was to be chosen from representatives of national minorities. Claiming that the ruling majority had sabotaged the election because their preferred candidate would not be chosen, four of the elected members resigned in December last year.

However, on July 10, parliament adopted an interpretation of the Law on Electronic Media clarifying that the resignations had no legal effect. Following this, the four members agreed to take up their seats on the REM Council, paving the way for it to be formally constituted.

On Monday, two candidates for the president’s position, Mileva Malesic and Milos Garic, won the same number of votes. Malesic was among the candidates who had resigned in December 2025.

Afterwards, Dubravka Valic Nedeljkovic, who chaired the meeting, said consultations would continue and a new session would be held soon.

“Until a president or chairperson is elected, the oldest member of the Council, which is me, will preside until a consensus is reached,” Valic Nedeljkovic said, adding that a president must be elected before the Council can begin to address the important issues concerning the REM.

EU reports on Serbia have repeatedly urged the REM Council to be established and start operating. The latest Rule of Law Report, published in July, said: “Serbia’s audiovisual market continued to face serious challenges in the absence of a functioning decision-making body of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media.”

Some of the problems that the Commission noted in the absence of a regulatory authority is that the competition for the allocation of the fifth frequency for national broadcasting, launched in 2022, has not yet concluded.

Some TV channels have started broadcasting on Telekom Srbija cable without the require licence, and have also received public funding, and public officials have appeared on them.

World.title: Bulgaria to Greenlight US Use of Air Base as Long-Term Hub
World.content:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev stated on Monday that parliament will likely authorise the presence of US aircraft at the Bezmer military base near Sofia.

Approval is likely to allow US aircraft passing through Sofia to refuel in relation to US operations in the Middle East to use the base long-term. On Tuesday, parliament’s defence committee will meet to kickstart the approval process.

Previously, in May, Radev criticised the presence of US aircraft at Sofia’s main Vassil Levski airport.

Radev had tried to hatch a deal with US President Donald Trump and allow a US presence at Sofia airport in exchange for the US lifting visa requirements on Bulgarian citizens. He eventually said he had “not received a positive answer” from Trump.

The Bezmer base is located around 260 kilometres from Sofia near the town of Yambol and is currently used by the Bulgarian Air Force – with which, before entering politics, Radev was a Major General and Commander. Bezmer had been previously used by US military in line with the Defence Cooperation Agreement between Bulgaria and the US signed in 2006.

The latest move fits Radev’s recent political manoeuvering between Washington, Brussels and Moscow.

Back in January he quit as President to successfully enter the race for parliament and assumed office as Prime Minister with his Progressive Bulgaria party, following a landslide win.

The foreign policy of Radev and Progressive Bulgaria is widely seen as being at odds with EU partners, but has also been flexible in practice. His government opposed the recent package of fresh EU sanctions on Russia, for example, but eventually decided not to veto them.

Earlier this month, Radev declined French President Emmanuel Macron’s invitation to attend the summit of the “Coalition of the Willing” aiding the defence of Ukraine. Radev said he did not see Bulgaria attending a summit that “insists on continuing financial and military aid to Ukraine”; however, on July 15, Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova took part in the 5th Ukraine-Southeast Europe Summit in Kyiv.

In a separate development, the Radev government was recently criticised for moves to close the commission that identifies people’s ties to communist-era security services.

World.title: Kosovo Prosecutorial Council Rejects Serb Prosecutors’ Return to Old Posts
World.content:
The Kosovo Prosecutorial Council meeting on July 20, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Prosecutorial System/Facebook Live/Screenshot.

The Kosovo Prosecutorial Council, KPC, on Monday denied the requests of several Serb prosecutors to return to their posts, nearly four years after Kosovo Serbs staged a mass resignation from Kosovo institutions in 2022.

Chief State Prosecutor Zejnullah Gashi told the KPC meeting on Monday that while he supported prosecutors from the Serb community being part of the system, he had not had time yet to familiarise himself with the matter.

“I stand by the position … that colleagues from the Serb community should also be part of the prosecutorial system. Regarding this topic or issue, I must honestly say that I was not informed in time, as I have only just assumed the role of Chief Prosecutor,” he said.

Media in Kosovo have reported that five prosecutors and 15 administrative staff members have asked to return.

KPC member Arlinda Muqa said the return of Serb prosecutors should not be treated as a political matter but solely as a legal issue.

“Kosovo has fulfilled all obligations arising from the agreements on the integration of the judiciary and the prosecution service. It provided them [Serbs] with the opportunity to become part of the constitutional system, enjoying all associated rights and professional guarantees. In 2022, they chose to resign; this constitutes a personal and legal act, the consequences of which are clearly defined by law,” she said.

Another KPC member, Visar Krasniqi, said: “As things stand, I cannot find grounds to support their return. I am convinced that the failure to verify their integrity is a serious issue, and I do not feel able to vote in favour of their return until time reveals whether these individuals were involved in activities that our own legislation does not recognise.”

Most Serbs in Kosovo’s four Serb-majority northern municipalities resigned on November 5, 2022, from their state posts, claiming that EU-mediated agreements between Serbia and Kosovo were being breached.

The resignations followed a meeting in the town of Zvecan organised by the Belgrade-backed party representing Kosovo Serbs, Srpska Lista.

Srpska Lista said the mayors of the Serb-majority municipalities, councillors, MPs, judges, prosecutors, judicial staff and Kosovo Police officers had all quit their jobs. During the meeting in Zvecan, Serb police officers symbolically took off their Kosovo police uniforms to applause from the participants.

The then leader of Srpska Lista, Goran Rakic, announcing the boycott of Kosovo’s institutions, said these decisions would remain in effect until an Association of Serb-Majority Municipalities, as agreed in the EU-facilitated Kosovo-Serbia dialogue, was established.

The move came two days after then regional director of the Kosovo Police for the Serb-majority north, Nenad Djuric, was suspended after he claimed that police in the north would not implement the government’s decision to issue reprimands to drivers of vehicles with licence plates issued by Serbia, which are considered illegal by the Kosovo authorities.

Sources told BIRN that the Kosovo Judicial Council has also received requests to return to work from several Serb judges. The exact number is not known.

After the 2022 boycott took effect, ethnic Albanians were elected as mayors in the north in extraordinary local elections in April 2023, on very low turnouts, after Serbs stayed away from the polls.

After these new mayors took office, the security situation in the north deteriorated. Clashes between protesters and NATO peacekeeping forces led to around 93 NATO personnel being injured, with one having a leg amputated.

Kosovo authorities also shut down a series of so-called “parallel” Serb institutions – services run outside government control – in the north of the country.

The European Union imposed some sanctions on Kosovo in June 2023 in response to the worsening security situation. These measures were lifted in March 2026.

Serb mayors retook power in the four Serb-majority municipalities in December 2025. During the election campaign, Srpska Lista admitted it had made a mistake in urging Serbs to abandon Kosovo institutions in 2022 – but said the decision had at least attracted the attention of the international community.

World.title: Croatian Clubs Discover Potential European Draws
World.content:
Croatia’s European hopefuls found out their possible third qualifying round opponents on Monday, with draws confirmed across the Europa League, Champions League, and Conference League paths.

Hajduk could face Salzburg

Should Hajduk get past Cypriot side Pafos in the second qualifying round of the Europa League, their reward will be a third-round clash with Austria’s Salzburg. Hajduk host Pafos in the first leg on Thursday in Split, with the return fixture in Cyprus the following Thursday. Should they progress, Hajduk would again have home advantage in the first leg of the third round, with the second leg to follow in Salzburg. Third qualifying round ties are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

Should Hajduk instead lose against Pafos, they would drop into the Conference League third qualifying round, where they’d face the winner of the tie between Georgia’s Dinamo Tbilisi and Lithuania’s Žalgiris, with the first leg played away from home.

Dinamo await Vikingur or Hapoel

Champions Dinamo Zagreb have also learned their potential path forward. Should they be eliminated by Switzerland’s Thun in the Champions League second qualifying round, Dinamo would drop into the Europa League third qualifying round to face either Iceland’s Vikingur or Israel’s Hapoel Beer Sheva.

Should Dinamo instead get past Thun and reach the Champions League third qualifying round itself, Mario Kovačević’s side would face the winner of the tie between Faroese side Klaksvik and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris, coached by Željko Sopić. First legs in that round are set for August 4/5, with second legs on August 11.

UEFA has scrapped the previous system of forming subgroups ahead of the “champions’ path” draw this season, meaning Dinamo faced a considerably wider pool of possible opponents than in previous years.

Before turning their attention to the third qualifying round, Dinamo first face Thun in the first leg of the second qualifying round on Tuesday in Switzerland, kicking off at 8 pm, with the return leg set for Tuesday, July 28.

Rijeka and Varaždin could head to Iceland

Rijeka and Varaždin also discovered their potential third qualifying round opponents in the Conference League on Monday. Rijeka, if they eliminate Ireland’s Derry City in the second round, would face the winner of the tie between Iceland’s Stjarnan and Finland’s Ilves. Varaždin, if they see off Czech side Jablonec, would take on the winner between Latvia’s RFS and Iceland’s Vestri.

Third qualifying round fixtures in the Conference League are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

World.title: Croatia vs Spain, Greece & Italy: Which Destination Comes Out on Top?
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – Croatia has become one of Europe’s most sought-after summer destinations, but how does it compare to the longtime tourism giants Spain, Greece and Italy?

As Vedran Salvia reports for Index, each country offers something unique, from world-famous beaches to ancient cities and exceptional cuisine. Despite the constantly evolving competition, Croatia appears to very successfully continue carving out its own niche, attracting travellers looking for crystal-clear waters, historic towns and a more relaxed coastal experience.

the croatian coast needs very little help in attracting attention

Croatia’s greatest strength remains its spectacular Adriatic coast. Stretching for more than 1,700 kilometres and dotted with over 1,200 islands, islets and reefs, it offers endless opportunities for sailing, island hopping and discovering secluded beaches. Unlike many Mediterranean destinations where development unfortunately totally dominates the coastline, much of Croatia’s shore remains remarkably well preserved, with national parks, hidden coves and picturesque, ancient fishing villages sitting alongside popular tourist hotspots like Dubrovnik, Split and Makarska.

how does that compare with spain?

Tourism heavyweight Spain continues to attract visitors with its vast array of long, sandy beaches, lively nightlife and major cities such as Barcelona, Valencia and Málaga. It also offers year-round sunshine in many regions. Croatia, however, appeals to travellers seeking a more intimate experience. While destinations like Dubrovnik can become crowded during peak season, much of the coastline remains quieter than Spain’s busiest resorts, particularly away from the best-known locations.

greece – the home of influencer islands

Nearby Greece is globally renowned for iconic, entirely different islands such as Santorini, Mykonos and Crete, along with its ancient history and rich Mediterranean cuisine. Croatia, located just up north, offers a different style of island holiday. Rather than focusing on a handful of internationally famous islands which have become totally swamped by influencers over more recent years (see Mykonos, for example), visitors can choose from hundreds of inhabited and uninhabited islands. Each of them has its very own character, from the lavender fields of Hvar’s interior and the vineyards of Korčula to the untouched nature of Mljet and Lastovo.

the home of the romans is hard to contend with, yet croatia manages to do so

Neighbouring Italy remains one of the world’s most visited countries thanks to remarkable cities such as Rome, Venice and Florence, alongside the Amalfi Coast and Sicily. The country that gave the world the Romans would be difficult to compete with for anyone, and yet Croatia, in its own way, still manages. Naturally, Croatia cannot match Italy’s sheer number of globally recognised cultural landmarks or its geographical size, but it often provides a similar Adriatic atmosphere at a more accessible price point. This is particularly true for sailing holidays, waterfront accommodation and seafood dining outside the very height of the summer season.

croatian prices – a gap that is narrowing (and quickly)

One of Croatia’s traditional advantages has always been affordability, although that gap has greatly narrowed in recent years. Since the country’s accession to the Eurozone, prices for accommodation, restaurants and tourism services have spiked noticeably, especially in popular coastal destinations. During the peak summer months, visitors may find Croatia approaching the prices of parts of Italy or Greece, particularly down in Dubrovnik, as well as in central Dalmatian destinations such as Hvar and Split. Despite that being the case, many lesser-known destinations continue to offer excellent value, particularly along the Kvarner coast, northern Dalmatia and of course away from the sea entirely in inland Croatia.

croatia is so much more than “just beaches”

Croatia’s appeal extends well beyond the coastline and 1,000+ islands. Visitors can explore the marvellous Plitvice Lakes National Park, hike through the imposing mountains of Velebit, discover a great many Roman monuments in Zadar, Pula and Split, sample world-class wines up in Istria and down Pelješac, or experience vibrant festivals and cultural events throughout the entire summer. Combined with its strong reputation as one of Europe’s safest destinations by far, these experiences continue to attract travellers looking for far more than a traditional beach holiday.

the verdict – croatia is the small country that could (and very much has)

Spain offers energy and variety, Italy delivers world-famous culture, and Greece remains synonymous with idyllic island escapes. Croatia, meanwhile, combines elements of all three: spectacular islands, historic towns, exceptional natural beauty and a coastline that remains one of the cleanest and most diverse in Europe. For travellers seeking a Mediterranean holiday that balances relaxation, adventure and history, Croatia continues to prove that it deserves its place alongside the region’s biggest tourism giants.

World.title: Europe’s Smallest Bible Is Hidden in Croatia, And It Fits in the Palm of Your Hand
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – You don’t have to be religious to appreciate the wonder of religious architecture and items, and one of the most fascinating (and tiny) items can be found in Croatia. Europe’s smallest Bible is actually hidden in a relatively overlooked part of Croatia.

Croatia is home to countless historical treasures, but few are as surprising as the smallest Bible in all of Europe, a tiny masterpiece that can fit comfortably in the palm of your hand. Putni kofer writes that this truly remarkable miniature Bible is kept in the town of Ludbreg, widely known as “the centre of the world” in northern Croatia, where it has become one of the area’s most unusual cultural attractions.

ludbreg – full of surprises

Despite its incredibly small dimensions, the Bible contains both the Old and New Testaments, printed in microscopic text and bound with exceptional craftsmanship. Its pages are so small that visitors are often astonished that an entire Bible could be produced in such a compact format, making it as much a feat of printing as it is an object of religious significance.

The miniature Bible forms part of Ludbreg’s exceptionally rich cultural and religious heritage. The town is already well known as one of Croatia’s most important pilgrimage destinations thanks to the Sanctuary of the Precious Blood of Christ, which attracts thousands of visitors each year, but this tiny book offers another fascinating reason to visit.

Visitors to Ludbreg are often surprised to discover that such a unique artefact is housed in a small Croatian town rather than in one of Europe’s larger museums.

more than a mere religious object

While the Bible’s size makes it an instant conversation piece, it also reflects the extraordinary skill of the printers and bookbinders who created it. Miniature books have long fascinated collectors around the world, but examples containing the complete biblical text are exceptionally rare, making Ludbreg’s specimen one of the continent’s most unusual literary treasures.

As touched on above, Ludbred is known as the “Centre of the World” thanks to a local legend. This small, humble northern Croatian continues to surprise visitors with attractions that extend far beyond its famous pilgrimage traditions. From its historic streets and castle to one of Europe’s tiniest Bibles, the town proves that some of Croatia’s most remarkable stories are found in places many international visitors have yet to discover.

World.title: Croatia Tightens Online Alcohol Sales With e-Citizens Age Verification
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – Croatia is continuing to fight its apparent war on alcohol sales from all angles, with mandatory e-Citizens age verification looming.

Purchasing alcohol online in Croatia is set to become significantly more secure after new rules introduced by the government require customers to verify their age through the e-Citizens (e-Građani) digital identity system before buying it. Poslovni reports that this latest measure is designed to prevent minors from buying alcoholic beverages online by introducing a reliable electronic age verification process, replacing the self-declaration methods commonly used by many online retailers today.

the age of digital id

Under the new rules, customers purchasing alcoholic drinks online will have to confirm they are of legal drinking age using Croatia’s e-Citizens platform. The digital verification system will allow retailers to confirm whether a customer is an adult without relying solely on manually entered dates of birth or simple tick-box declarations, which have long been criticised as ineffective.

In traditional shops, retailers are obviously already required to refuse alcohol sales to minors and can ask customers to present identification if they doubt their age. The new system aims to bring online alcohol sales closer to those same standards by ensuring age verification takes place before the transaction is completed. Officials say the change reflects the growing importance of digital commerce and the need to apply the same consumer protection rules regardless of whether alcohol is purchased in person or online.

online retailers should have the exact same level of responsibility

Businesses selling alcoholic beverages over the internet will now need to integrate the e-Citizens verification process into their online stores. The move is expected to improve legal certainty for retailers while making it considerably more difficult for underage users to bypass age restrictions through false declarations.

The introduction of mandatory digital age verification is another example of Croatia expanding the use of its e-Citizens platform beyond mere public administration into everyday commercial services. Over the past decade, the platform has become a central gateway for accessing government services, digital documents and official records. Its use for online age verification reflects a broader shift towards secure digital identity solutions that are becoming increasingly common across Europe.

For consumers, the biggest change will be simple: anyone buying alcohol online in Croatia should expect to log in through e-Citizens before placing an order for alcohol, adding an extra step designed to ensure that alcohol is sold only to adults.

World.title: Zagreb Bus Station Set for Major Renovation as First Phase Gets Underway
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – The now quite dated and dilapidated Zagreb bus station is set to undergo a major renovation as the first phase finally gets underway.

Zagreb bus station is set to undergo a long-awaited modernisation, with the first phase of renovation focusing on improving passenger facilities and upgrading key parts of one of Croatia’s busiest transport hubs.

AKZ.hr reports that this significant investment marks the beginning of a broader effort to revitalise the station, which has served millions of passengers for decades and remains the country’s largest hub for domestic and international bus travel.

The initial phase of works will prioritise improvements that passengers use every day, including the station’s waiting areas, sanitary facilities and other public spaces that have shown signs of age after years of heavy use. Station management has claimed that the primary goal is to improve comfort, accessibility and the overall travel experience while ensuring the terminal remains fully operational throughout the renovation process.

modernising a crucial national transport hub

Opened back in 1987, Zagreb bus station handles thousands of passengers each day and connects the Croatian capital with destinations across Croatia and Europe. Despite its importance, much of the complex has remained largely unchanged for decades, prompting growing calls for refurbishment as passenger expectations and transport standards have evolved. The planned upgrades are expected to improve both the appearance and functionality of the station while extending the lifespan of the existing infrastructure.

The renovation is being presented as the first stage of a wider modernisation programme that could eventually include additional commercial spaces, energy-efficiency improvements and further infrastructure upgrades. By carrying out the work in phases, operators aim to minimise disruption while gradually bringing the station up to modern standards.

As Croatia continues investing in transport infrastructure as a whole, from railways and airports to roads and public transport, the refurbishment of Zagreb bus station represents yet another concerted effort to modernise the country’s key mobility hubs. For the millions of passengers who pass through the station each and every year, the first phase of works is expected to deliver noticeable improvements while laying the groundwork for a more comprehensive transformation in the years ahead.

World.title: Driving Licence Reform Looms in Croatia as Digital Licences Move Closer
World.content:
July the 20th, 2026 – A major driving license reform is on the horizon in Croatia as digital licenses move closer to becoming a new reality.

Croatian drivers could soon see one of the biggest changes to driving licences in very many decades as the European Union moves towards introducing a digital driving licence that will be recognised across all member states.

Poslovni reports that the aforementioned reform forms part of a broader overhaul of EU driving licence rules designed to simplify cross-border recognition, improve road safety and modernise the way motorists prove their driving entitlement. Croatia, as an EU member state, will be required to implement the new framework once it is formally adopted.

digital driving licenses will become the new norm

Under the new rules, drivers will be able to store their driving licence in a secure digital format on their smartphone through the forthcoming European Digital Identity Wallet. The digital version will become the default across the European Union, although motorists will still be able to request a traditional physical licence if they prefer. The aim is to make licences easier to renew, verify and use when travelling between EU countries.

new rules for young and older drivers

The reform package also introduces several measures intended to improve road safety. Among them is a probationary period of at least two years for newly qualified drivers, during which stricter penalties will apply for serious traffic offences such as drink driving or failing to wear a seatbelt. EU countries are also being encouraged to introduce accompanied driving schemes for seventeen-year-olds to help young motorists gain experience before driving independently.

The updated legislation also harmonises validity periods for driving licences and includes new provisions relating to medical fitness to drive, although individual member states will retain flexibility in how health assessments are carried out.

easier eu-wide recognition

One of the key objectives of the reform is to make life easier for people living, working or travelling across Europe. A standardised digital licence will allow authorities throughout the entire bloc to recognise driving entitlements more efficiently while reducing bureaucracy for drivers moving between member states.

For Croatian motorists, the changes will obviously not happen overnight. The legislation must first complete the final stages of the EU legislative process before member states begin implementing the new system. Once introduced, however, the reform will mark the most significant change to driving licences in decades, replacing paper-based administration with a digital-first system designed for an increasingly connected European Union while keeping physical licences available for those who still want them.

World.title: Fewer Foreigners Moving to Croatia as Immigration Slows in Early 2026
World.content:
July the 20th, 2026 – Fewer and fewer foreigners have been recorded as moving to Croatia as the immigration from third countries we’ve witnessed over recent years eases throughout early 2026.

Following on from several years of record immigration from distant (primarily Asian) countries driven largely by labour shortages, the number of people moving to Croatia has begun to slow. This has been concluded following a deep dive into the latest figures released by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS).

This brand new data shows that while Croatia has been continuing to record positive net migration, both immigration and emigration declined during the first half of 2026. That suggests that the rapid influx of foreign workers seen over more recent years may finally be starting to stabilise.

According to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, fewer people moved to Croatia compared with the same period last year. Foreign workers continue to account for the vast majority of new arrivals, reflecting ongoing demand in sectors such as construction, tourism, hospitality, manufacturing and transport. However, the pace of arrivals has eased compared to the exceptional growth recorded over the past two years.

most foreigners moving to croatia so far in 2026 continue to come from the country’s immediate region

The largest number of foreign nationals relocating to Croatia continue to come from neighbouring countries and Southeast Asia. Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Nepal remain among the biggest groups of newcomers, with workers from the Philippines and India also continuing to play an increasingly important role in Croatia’s labour market. Many are employed in industries facing persistent shortages of domestic workers, particularly seasonal tourism and construction.

croatia’s enfeebled labour market remains the main driver

Croatia has experienced a dramatic increase in labour migration since the abolition of annual foreign worker quotas and the rapid expansion of work permit approvals. A rapidly ageing population, record low unemployment and sustained demand from employers have encouraged companies to recruit workers from abroad, transforming Croatia from a country traditionally associated with emigration into one increasingly dependent on foreign labour. Although immigration has slowed, it does have to be noted that employers in several sectors continue to report difficulties filling vacancies without international recruitment.

the positive migration trend is continuing – for now

Despite the decline in arrivals, Croatia continues to record more people moving into the country than leaving it.

Demographers note that positive net migration is an important development for a country that spent decades experiencing population decline through emigration. However, they also point out that immigration alone cannot fully offset Croatia’s long-term demographic challenges, including low birth rates and an ageing population. With tourism, infrastructure projects and economic growth continuing to fuel demand for workers, foreign labour is expected to remain an essential part of Croatia’s economy, even if the pace of immigration becomes more moderate than in recent years.

World.title: Croatian Landlords Accuse Government of “Campaigning Against Them”
World.content:
July the 20th, 2026 – Croatian landlords who rent out private accommodation units to tourists are still feeling targeted and now openly accusing the government of campaigning against them.

Representatives of Croatia’s private accommodation sector have stepped up their open and clear criticism of recent government tourism reforms, arguing that a series of new regulations and taxes are placing an unfair burden on family-run rentals while doing little to solve the country’s wider housing challenges.

The comments come amid an increasingly heated national debate over the future of Croatia’s tourism model, with policymakers seeking to reduce pressure on the housing market while encouraging higher-quality and more sustainable tourism development. Ivica Brkljaca writes for Index that the centre of the dispute are the country’s hundreds of thousands of private accommodation beds, which have long formed the backbone of Croatia’s tourism industry.

a pushback from industry representatives

Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ), recently described the structure of Croatia’s accommodation sector as one of the country’s biggest tourism challenges, noting that private accommodation accounts for a particularly large share of available beds. He argued that recent government measures should be viewed as long-term reforms aimed at improving the sustainability of the tourism sector.

However, organisations representing Croatian private landlords say they feel increasingly targeted by new legislation and public rhetoric. They argue that family accommodation providers are being blamed for issues such as housing shortages and overtourism despite operating legally and contributing significantly to local economies, particularly in coastal communities. According to critics, the reforms risk discouraging ordinary households that rely on seasonal tourism income.

rising costs pose a serious issue

Among the industry’s biggest concerns are higher lump-sum taxes, additional administrative requirements and new rules affecting short-term rentals, particularly in apartment buildings. Various landlord associations argue that many family-run businesses operate only during the summer season and on relatively modest earnings, making it increasingly difficult to absorb additional financial and regulatory obligations. They warn that some owners may ultimately decide to leave the market altogether.

Supporters of the reforms argue that Croatia needs to shift away from relying overwhelmingly on private accommodation and encourage investment in hotels and higher-value tourism products. Critics disagree, saying reducing the number of private rentals through administrative measures would simply shrink accommodation capacity during peak season, potentially driving prices even higher rather than improving affordability or extending the tourist season. They also argue there is little evidence that fewer private apartments would automatically increase hotel occupancy outside the summer months.

an uncertain future lies ahead in the eyes of many

With new tourism legislation continuing to be rolled out, the debate over Croatia’s now historic accommodation model is unlikely to subside anytime soon. While the government maintains that the reforms are designed to create a more balanced and sustainable tourism sector, many small landlords remain unconvinced, insisting they are being asked to shoulder a disproportionate share of the changes despite playing a central role in Croatia’s tourism success for decades.

World.title: Katrina Lehis, Estonia épée teams open Fencing World Championships
World.content:
World number one women's fencer Katrina Lehis along with the rest of the national team is poised to take part Fencing World Championships in Hong Kong this week.

Estonia is competing in both the women's and men's épée events, and world titles in both individual and team events are

Women's team head coach Nikolai Novosjolov said ahead of the competition that preparations had gone according to plan.

"The competitive conditions are very good, and everything needed for successful preparation is in place. As of now the work has been done, and now it is time to compete. Our greatest strength is the members of the women's team themselves – I believe they are ready to show their level," Novosjolov said.

As world number one, Lehis has automactically qualified for round one, the round of 64, while her teammates, Irina Embrich, Julia Beljajeva and Veronika Zuikova have to go through qualifying Wednesday.

All four men: Sten Priinits, Kasper Tafenau, Oliver Laasik and Markus Salm, have to go through qualifying.

Priinits said the team had been able to prepare well and that morale was high. "We have been able to do high-quality training sessions and sparring with athletes from different countries. I believe the entire team is ready to give 100 percent," he said.

The World Fencing Championships start Wednesday, July 22 and run until Thursday, July 30, and are being held in Hong Kong for the first time. The competition has attracted over a thousand competitors from over 100 countries will compete.

The women's individual events run July 22-25, the men's start and end a day later. The women's team event is on July 28, the men's on July 29. The event's official site is here.

World.title: Estonia to shift to mostly two-person ambulance crews by 2028
World.content:
Estonia's ambulance service is to be overhauled and a more streamlined structure will enter work from 2028, mostly using two-person crews and aimed at regional standardization.

Two state bodies, the Health Board (Tervisamet) and the Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa) are developing the new model, which they said in a joint statement will position ambulance crews more closely in line with actual demand, and will bring emergency care closer to people.

Regional disparities will be reduced, the authorities said. As well as mostly two-person crews staffing ambulances, there will be fewer ambulance teams working nights, under the 2028 new plan.

"This is a more flexible deployment and operating model, allowing ambulance crews to be positioned closer to people and providing better coverage in areas where the current network does not ensure sufficiently even access," the Health Insurance Fund and the Health Board said in a joint statement.

For more serious cases, resuscitation units are planned to support ambulance crews, while physician support teams will be added in every region.

The two authorities said that adding physician support teams to regional Estonia will help standardize service quality and improve the handling of more complex cases throughout Estonia. "Medical expertise will no longer be concentrated solely in the larger centers, but will become more flexibly available across the regions. In addition, development of telemedicine support and the e-ambulance system for ambulance crews will continue, helping ensure the provision of a uniform ambulance service throughout Estonia," the statement went on.

Specialized capabilities will be important under the new model. Field supervisors, first response teams, physician support teams and resuscitation units will be available across Estonia to assist ambulance crews treating critically ill patients, during peak demand and at complex incidents.

"First response teams have an important role on the smaller islands, where maintaining a permanent full-scale ambulance crew is not practical given population distribution and call volumes. A local team can begin providing care before additional ambulance resources arrive or before the patient is transported," the statement continued. Areas where weather conditions, geography or transport connections may affect response times are to be particularly in focus.

Under the 2028 network model, new ambulance bases will be added in four regions of Estonia. Healthcare authorities will select locations based on where they most improve emergency care access, considering distances, population distribution, call volumes and response times.

The Health Board and Health Insurance Fund note ambulance workload varies by time of day. In 2025, 64 percent of call-outs occurred during daytime and 36 percent at night. Therefore, the new model expands the daytime network, while reducing night crews but maintaining emergency care readiness across Estonia, authorities emphasized, with emergency coverage preserved throughout the country despite fewer overnight units.

Estonia will retain medical ambulance services, with nurse- or doctor-led crews and healthcare status maintained.

The new network model will primarily use two-person ambulance crews, while three-person crews will remain in areas and situations requiring them.

The Health Insurance Fund plans to announce a public tender for new ambulance service funding contracts no later than September 30 this year, to replace the current ambulance service contracts, which expire on the last day of next year.

Ambulance provision is organized on a regional basis.

World.title: Turkish Airlines suspected of using Russian airspace on flight from Tallinn
World.content:
A Turkish Airlines aircraft operating a passenger flight from Tallinn to Istanbul on 12 July allegedly ended up over Russian territory during the flight.

The aircraft changed its usual route and flew over the Kaliningrad region, although flights normally avoid Russian airspace, writes the online edition of the weekly Eesti Ekspress.

One passenger said he noticed the route change in a flight‑tracking app and approached a flight attendant. After consulting the pilots, he was told that flying over Kaliningrad was a deliberate decision by the crew, as they considered this route the most optimal.

Lennuliiklusteeninduse AS, the company responsible for air‑traffic management in Estonia, said that according to the approved flight plan, the route should have passed through Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, without entering Russian airspace.

The head of the aviation department at Estonia's Ministry of Climate, Taivo Linnamägi, emphasized that flights over Russian territory are considered unsafe for civil aviation due to the ongoing war and the risks associated with it.

Although Turkish Airlines has the right to use Russian airspace, Flightradar data shows that such a route is rather an exception for flights between Tallinn and Istanbul.

Representatives of Turkish Airlines have not commented the incident, Eesti Ekspress said.

World.title: Mihkel Mariusz Jezierski: Students expect clear rules for using AI
World.content:
Discussions held with roughly a thousand Estonian high school students revealed one important conclusion: the need for clearer agreements on the use of artificial intelligence in learning. Uncertainty is students' biggest concern, writes Mihkel Mariusz Jezierski.

From March to May, 950 high school students in 18 Estonian schools took part in world‑café discussions about the role of artificial intelligence in school and its impact on learning, relationships, creativity, social‑media use and their sense of the future.

In Estonia, discussions often focus on how AI affects learning, but much less on how it affects education as a whole: relationships, creativity, the information environment and perceptions of the future. School is not only a place where knowledge is acquired, but an environment where a person develops. Therefore, the role of AI must be assessed much more broadly than through learning outcomes alone.

Although students are the first to experience AI's impact every day, they are rarely included in discussions about what role AI should have in school. The world‑café sessions aimed to fill that gap.

Uncertainty creates unfairness

Students say that schools and teachers differ greatly in how they handle AI use. Some teachers ban AI entirely, while others actively encourage it. Students feel a sense of unfairness — and reduced trust in teacher‑created materials — when a teacher uses AI to create learning materials but forbids students from using the same tool.

Uncertainty also creates unfairness in assessment, students say. They described situations where independently completed work received a lower grade than work done with AI, because the teacher found it difficult to distinguish the student's contribution from AI's. When a grade no longer reflects a student's actual knowledge or effort, assessment loses part of its meaning in students' eyes.

"They described situations where independently completed work received a lower grade than work done with AI."

A similar uncertainty concerns creative work. Only 21 percent of students believe that a result created with AI is fully their own. Creativity is often tied to self‑determination and a sense of ownership. Many high school students want clear guidance on how to use AI in ways that support idea development without replacing the creative process or becoming the source of ideas itself. They also need instructions on how to describe and cite AI's contribution in their work.

For this reason, students expect to work with teachers to write down agreements that define when, how and to what extent AI may be used in learning. One of the goals of the AI‑Leap student program for the next school year is to help shape such shared agreements in every Estonian school.

The AI‑Leap initiative does not aim to restrict AI use, but to help find solutions that support learning and keep school primarily a human‑created environment rather than one shaped around technology.

Exclusion may encourage misuse of AI

AI provides quick, non‑judgmental answers. For many students, it is easier to turn to AI than to a teacher, parent or peer — especially when they fear making mistakes. It turned out that about one‑third of high school students seek help from AI first when a problem arises, although one‑fifth do so rarely or have never turned to AI.

Students say misuse of chatbots occurs more often among peers who have mental‑health concerns or difficulties with communication. The weaker the emotional support and sense of belonging, the more likely a young person is to replace normal interaction with AI.

At the same time, high school students emphasize that AI should not and cannot replace a human as a communication partner. They see the solution in strengthening the school's social role: because AI makes learning increasingly individual, schools should support communication and community feeling more than before and ensure mental‑health support.

I believe that AI's impact on education should not be assessed only through learning outcomes. School is where relationships, belonging and young people themselves take shape. The more individual AI makes learning, the more important it is to keep school a human‑designed environment.

Personalized learning must not make school more lonely

AI enables more personalized learning than before, but we must ask how this affects students' relationships, cooperation and sense of belonging when each learner moves increasingly along their own individual learning path together with AI.

Educational technology should not personalize only learning — it should also help maintain the relationships and shared experiences through which a school becomes a community. This does not have to hinder innovation. But these are principles that must be considered in developing any AI solution for education, including further development of AI‑Leap's Socratic learning application ITI.

The world‑café discussions also highlighted concerns about social‑media algorithms, which students say increasingly shape their worldview and information consumption. Young people also feel uncertainty about the future, because AI is changing the labor market and required skills. They want schools to teach more media literacy, the principles behind algorithms, and skills for adapting to a rapidly changing world.

High school students' message to their schools is that above all they expect the opportunity to formulate clear agreements on AI use together with teachers. They also consider important a school culture that values making mistakes and learning from them, accessible mental‑health support, individual feedback, and transparent labeling of AI use.

World.title: 19th century Estonian settlers in Caucasus linked malaria to hard work, raw berries
World.content:
An Estonian National Museum (ERM) expert has shed light on how Estonian settlers in the Caucasus region dealt with the scourge of malaria, at a time when the illness was poorly understood.

Estonians settled primarily along the Black Sea coast of the Caucasus region, including in Abkhazia, in the late 19th to early 20th centuries. Like Estonia itself, the area was part of the Tsarist Empire before World War One.

At the time, malaria, a deadly disease, was not fully understood and while quinine was available, sometimes folk remedies were chosen ahead of it by the Estonian arrivals.

Whereas today, the fact that malaria gets spread by mosquitoes is common knowledge, anti-malarial tablets were some decades off and many Estonians who moved to the Caucasus region over a century ago blamed the deadly disease on damp ground, raw berries or even excessive hard work.

The new overview has been assembled by ERM senior researcher Aivar Jürgenson, who studied settlers' correspondence, memoirs and newspaper articles from the late 19th to early 20th centuries, prior to Estonia's independence. His findings were reported also in the journal Philological Researches.

Caucasus Estonians in nature. Source: RA/EFA.505.0.154300

Soon after the villages of Linda, Estonia, Salme and Sulevi were established by Estonian settlers in Abkhazia in the 1880s, malaria became one of the deadliest enemies for the new residents.

More than half of the arriving emigrants contracted the disease and were taken seriously ill, and nearly 16 percent of the settlements' populations died of malaria.

Because science had not at that time discovered the connection between mosquitoes and malaria, the settlers believed in prevailing theories of the time. According to these, malaria emanated as a poisonous vapor from damp ground and swamps. To combat this, houses began to be built on stilts, so that air might pass beneath the floors. Eucalyptus trees were planted to dry the ground, and swamps were drained. Since this deprived mosquitoes of their breeding grounds, this did serve to curb the incidence of malaria, albeit not for the reasons understood.

Descriptions also revealed the impact malaria had on a central tenet of Estonian national pride: Namely the work ethic. Obviously those suffering from malaria could not work, but the arrivals had also seen local inhabitants as "lazy." When ethnic Estonians started falling ill too, another misguided conclusion emerged – the belief that a person from northerly climes simply could not withstand strenuous labor in a hotter climate.

Only later was it grasped that it was malaria itself that was exhausting people. The folly of eating raw berries and drinking water which had not been boiled first were soon added to the supposed list of causes of malaria.

Malaria is carried by mosquitoes, though this was not understood in the late 19th century. Source: Egor Kamelev/Unsplash

As well as the attributed causes, the methods used to treat malaria at the time reveal a colorful blend of folk tradition and contemporary medicine. Imported from Estonia was another belief: That malaria was a spirit in the shape of a gray old man that had to be driven away or frightened. For this reason, the malaise was known as "Halltõbi" ("Gray disease").

Supposed cures included rolling around in the straw in a pigsty, or keeping pieces of crosses collected from cemeteries under the left side of the body while sleeping.

The properties of quinine, originally from the New World, were known about by this time, at least to medical professionals, and doctors did start prescribing this plant-based treatment.

However, many Estonian arrivals not only found quinine's bitter taste – familiar to many today in tonic water, which it is a key ingredient of – unpalatable, they also mistakenly believed that the medicine was poisonous, opting to consume locally made wine instead in an effort to cure the disease's ravages.

Malaria still exists and WHO data states in 2024 there were around 282 million malaria cases, and 610,000 deaths as a result of the disease, chiefly in Africa.

Symptoms can be both mild and life-threatening. Mild symptoms include fever, chills and headache. Severe symptoms include fatigue, confusion, seizures, and difficulty breathing. Prophylactic medicines can be taken ahead of visiting a region known to have cases of malaria, and care should be taken to avoid mosquito bites, including by using repellents and netting.

World.title: EU won't revise ETS2, Commission official tells Estonia
World.content:
Infringement proceedings have already been launched against the member states that have not transposed the extended emissions trading system ETS2, said Helena Braun, head of the policy division at the European Commission Representation in Estonia.

ETS2 is a new carbon pricing cap-and-trade system created by the European Union to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from road transport, buildings, and additional small industrial sectors. Original EU ETS targets heavy industry and large power plants.

The Estonian government has previously been critical of ETS2, and Prime Minister Kristen Michal said already in mid‑June that it should be postponed.

Last week, Prime Minister Michal said the aim is to cancel it altogether.

"The desire to achieve the goals is understandable, and I am generally on the side of new technology and a cleaner environment, but this is simply too bureaucratic to succeed, or at least to succeed in a meaningful way," Michal said, adding that this is also the official position of the government and the state.

Commission sees no reason for change

"Everything is theoretically possible, but at the moment the European Commission sees no reason to put a new amendment proposal on the table," said Helena Braun, head of the policy division at the European Commission Representation in Estonia.

Braun said that 18 EU member states have already transposed ETS2 into national law, three have done so partially, and six have not. Estonia is among the latter group and submitted, together with nine other countries, a request to review ETS.

Citizens of EU member states generally support the Union's climate goals. On average, support for the EU's 2050 climate‑neutrality target stands at 81 percent.

In Estonia, however, the figure is only 46 percent — the lowest in the EU.

Since Estonia is strongly opposed to the system, what would happen if Estonia does not adopt it by 2027?

"The European Commission opens infringement proceedings against a member state if agreed EU law has not been transposed into national law. This infringement procedure is currently ongoing, and we do not comment further on the content of ongoing procedures," Braun said.

Through infringement proceedings, the Commission applies legal measures against member states that have not fulfilled obligations arising from EU law.

In the first phase, the Commission sends the country a formal notice, to which it must respond within two months and commit to remedying the violation.

If the Commission considers the response insufficient or the violation continues, it sends a reasoned opinion in the second phase, describing precisely the nature of the violation and giving a new deadline (usually two months) to correct the situation.

Other adjustments needed

According to Braun, Europe's energy price level is very high compared with, for example, the United States, and the reason is that Europe must buy more than half of its consumed energy from third countries.

"Since 2022, when Russia launched its full‑scale war against Ukraine, Russia used Europe's heavy dependence as a weapon. Today we see the same in the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Since the closure of the strait, Europe has paid 50 billion euros more for energy without receiving a single extra molecule. Fifty billion is an enormous amount of money that we could have invested in our economy and in people," Braun said.

The Commission wants to extend the distribution of free allowances to energy‑intensive industries, such as steel and cement production. This would apply until 2038.

According to Braun, the extension aims to protect European industry more strongly and give these sectors breathing room. However, the free allowances would not be unconditional: companies would receive 80 percent of the allowances if they have a concrete plan for cleaner production, and the remaining 20 percent once investments have been made according to the plan.

Previously, each country could allocate its ETS revenue essentially wherever it wished. This meant member states could use it, for example, to patch budget holes or invest in infrastructure.

In the future, however, at least 50 percent of the revenue must go back to the sector from which it originated. According to Braun, only five percent of ETS revenue has gone back to those sectors so far.

"It will no longer be entirely up to member states to decide where they direct ETS revenue," she said, adding that 50 percent of the revenue would still go toward supporting a just transition and helping people through the process.

Braun said she could not yet say whether ETS changes might raise the price of heating or waste collection in Estonia.
